speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, this afternoon I will direct the main body of my comments to two particular issues. One is the Amax Corporation, which is the Alice Arm dumping station, and the other is the Kemano completion. These two issues have a very real impact upon the fishing industry in that they relate to a reduction in salmon spawning and rearing grounds, and, combined with pollution, they are two of the most pressing and serious problems facing the fishing industry in Canada today.
1 think it is important all members of the House, particularly those members on the government side, keep in mind what is happening to the Canadian environment in relation to the serious threat posed by acid rain to 20,000 lakes in Ontario and Quebec, the very serious pollution in the Great Lakes and most of the rivers in Canada, and the fact that unless we have some very serious moves in terms of environmental protection, not only in our rivers and lakes but in our near-shore marine areas in the oceans in the maritimes, British Columbia and the Arctic, very soon we will not have a fishing industry on which to stand and debate in the House.
This is not to underplay the serious economic problems which face the industry from overcapitalization, high interest rates and so on, but stock reductions throughout Canada from inadequate environmental and habitat protection are at the core of the disaster facing our fishing industry today. The pollution of our inland waters, the Great Lakes, the maritimes, the Arctic and the Pacific coast, along with the litany of developments ranging from Riley Creek in British Columbia to mercury pollution in the Wabigoon and English River system are signals that the fishery in Canada does not have or use the mandate given to it by the public interest.
Let me first deal with Amax, the Alice Arm situation in British Columbia, which I have raised in this House on a number of occasions in the past year. It relates to a special dumping permit, SOR-79-345, which was brought in April 10, 1979, in mid-election, as a result of a backroom cabinet deal between the Liberal party and the Amax Corporation. This permit allows the direct dumping of 100 million metric tons of effluent into Alice Arm, which is an area of substantial importance to the commercial and native fisheries on the northern B.C. coast. Some of the effluent is composed of arsenic, copper, lead, nickel, zinc, radium-226 and cadmium. I intend to deal in some detail this afternoon with one of those elements.
The Department of Fisheries and Oceans and the Department of the Environment, I would point out, have investigated
the possibility of on-land tailings disposal and have found it not only feasible but have found that only a 2 per cent difference in return on investment is required to have a relatively benign environmental on-land tailings disposal. The difference, I would point out to hon. members, is $29 million for on-land tailings versus $6 million for direct dumping into the ocean.
I think it is important that all members keep in mind that what the Department of Fisheries and Oceans has decided is adequate for an acute lethality test is to place a number of rainbow trout fingerlings into a tank, run some effluent into it, and if not more than half the fish die within 96 hours, then the bioassay sample passes. I think that is a very questionable way of testing the impact on a commercial or a food fishery resource.
I would like to place on record today some excerpts from the Environmental Health Committee of the British Columbia Medical Association on just one of the elements of this 100 million metric tons federal government dumping. The radium-226 summary says:
-about 1 millionth of a gram (I microgram-Mg) or 35 billionths of an ounce in the body, can cause bone cancer
-radium leaches into the environment much more readily after the ore is ground up than when it is embedded in solid rock. It is fairly mobile in the environment
-chemicals used in the milling process may further increase the leachability of radium-226
-radium-226 is concentrated in the food chain Cancer Causing Dose -radium-226 is the second most toxic radioactive bone cancer producing substance after radioactive plutonium-239. It is between 10-100 times more carcinogenic than radioactive strontium-90.
-the lowest dose of radium-226 that has been found to cause bone cancer in man is 1.2 micro curies which is equivalent to 1.2 micrograms or 1.2 millionths of a curie or gram.
The summary goes on to refer to "Biological Pathways and Food Chain Concentration", which is crucial-and it is unfortunate the Minister of Fisheries and Oceans (Mr. LeBlanc) is not here today. However, I am sure that members over on that side of the House will transmit this information back to him, which relates to a dumping permit he granted in a backroom cabinet deal with this corporation.
The summary goes on:
A great variety of oceanic organisms accumulate radium far in excess of that present in sea water. Some marine micro-organisms (example diatoms) concentrate radium-226 from 1,000 to 3,000 times seawater levels.
The Department of Fisheries and Oceans is only requiring that the actual level in the sea water be monitored.
There is a great deal of research needed to demonstrate the mechanisms by which radium is concentrated as it goes up the food chain from increased water levels to aquatic plants, phytoplankton and diatoms, to fish and then to animals and man; or from increased water levels to terrestial plants, then animals and man.
I point out to members opposite that these are questions which have really not been looked into at all by the government in giving out this very unusual permit. As a matter of fact it is the only one of its kind to be granted to a mining corporation in Canada.
October 27, 1980

1 will read from one of the documents upon which the cabinet based its decision. Under the heading, "Existing Regulatory Requirements under the Fisheries Act", it says:
These regulations, which were promulgated in February, 1977, prohibit the deposit of effluents (including tailings) with a suspended solids level greater than 25 ppm.
1 would point out that the Minister of Fisheries and Oceans in his recommendation last year to the cabinet put in 400,000 parts per million in this special dumping permit. The document continues:
Therefore, if the marine disposal option is to be authorized pursuant to the Fisheries Act, a special, site-specific regulation for this operation would have to be developed and passed by the governor in council upon recommendation of the Minister of Fisheries and Oceans.
The Department of the Environment and the Department of Fisheries and Oceans are, in general, opposed to the unconfined disposal of tailings. Flowever, the policy of the departments has been to acknowledge that the practice can be authorized under special extenuating circumstances.
The most recent departmental position with regard to this issue was presented in January, 1978, to the B.C. Pollution Control Board Inquiry into the development of the province's mining, milling and smelting effluent objectives. 1 quote from that presentation as follows:
To protect the Canadian fisheries, the federal cabinet endorsed the policy of containment of pollutants at source based on the installation of the best practicable control technology. However, it has been recognized by the Environmental Protection Service of Environment Canada that under special circumstances it is virtually impossible to install the required control technology-
And here we come to the economic factors, the deal on which the Liberals obviously made their decision:
-the Department of the Environment, on the basis of its review of January 1979 data, believes that the construction of such a tailings pond on land can be economically feasible. Regardless of whether the 1978 or the 1979 prices are considered, there is approximately a 2 per cent difference in the return on investment between on-land disposal and marine disposal of tailings.
So the government is on record as saying that a tailings pond can be designed and developed, can be maintained at only 2 per cent return difference on investment, and they opted for the latter, the cheaper $6 million direct-ocean dumping which, as I will point out in a few moments, has a terrible impact on the commercial and food fisheries in that area.
I go on to quote from the same document with respect to submarine disposal into Alice Arm:
-The potential for heavy metal buildup in the food chain to the point where there may be an impact upon the ecosystem, including man.
A report done by a biologist in British Columbia was released last week. It was called the McCart report. 1 quote from page 18 of that report:
The commercial fishery would be expected to benefit by about $4.25 million over the 26-year life of the mine, ignoring the possibility of price increases.
One of the things which has certainly not been looked at by the Minister of Fisheries and members on that side is the impact of 100 million tonnes of effluent going into the inlet. It is going to smother life on the bottom of the inlet and will spread up to the surface and cause serious problems in terms
Fishing Industry
of heavy metal building and poisoning of various other fish species.
With regard to shrimp densities, I quote from page 29 of the McCart report. This shows some of the very serious flaws in the scientific evidence upon which the government based its decision. In relation to shrimp, I quote:
The confidence limits, expressed as a percentage of the mean, were plus or minus 188.5 per cent.
How anyone in their right mind, particularly the Minister of Fisheries and Oceans, could support a proposal going ahead when there was that sort of confidence limits is certainly, at the very best, questionable.
The conclusion of the McCart report says it all in my view. On page 68 it says:
The potential impacts are serious enough to preclude the marine disposal of tailings.
One of the groups which will be most seriously impacted, other than the commercial fishermen, are the Nishga people who live in that area. In the community of Kincolith, for example, its vice-president made a statement a few weeks ago. He is Mr. Rod Robinson of the Nishga Tribal Council, and he said:
The company has offered us a share in the mine. Our share is death.
That is certainly something that neither the Minister of Fisheries nor members on that side have responded to, to date. It was predicted that if the tailings were confined to depths greater than 100 metres the following would probably occur: (a) most of the area of Alice Arm to Hans Point will eventually be blanketed with tailings; (c) the productivity of deep water benthos fauna including commercially exploitable species such as shrimps, prawns, various species of king crab, as well as demersal fish such as halibut, rock fish, crab etc. will be reduced or where deposition is very heavy, entirely eliminated.
At this point I would quote from statements of Mr. Born, President of Amax, and by Mr. Lenton, the General Manager. First, Mr. Born:
The marine disposal, in the opinion of expert marine consultants and federal and provincial environmental officials, will have no detrimental effect on the marine life in the area and will not harm the salmon fishery.
I quote from Mr. Lenton:
The tailing will have no adverse impact on the environment in Alice Arm.
It is interesting to have a look at what other people have said, people who are perhaps not biased by having some tie, as the Liberals do, to the $23 million which they have saved Amax or the corporation in its direct interest. I quote from Stephen Pond, a University of British Columbia physiological oceanographer, who says:
There is evidence that heavier, saltier water from outside the inlet flows in, mixing up the water. The prediction made that the material would go down to the bottom and stay there is not likely to hold true.
In August, 1980, bishops of the Anglican Church and bishops of the Catholic Church in Canada called for a with-

October 27, 1980
Fishing Industry
drawal of the special order in council and for a moratorium upon development of the resource until technology is developed to dispose of the tailings safely. I point out that the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) has not responded to either the bishops of the Anglican Church or the bishops of the Catholic Church regarding their very serious questions and allegations on the Amax project in British Columbia.
I quote from Dr. Albright, a microbiologist from Simon Fraser University:
We cannot accept the argument that aquatic animals have adapted to high turbidities or heavy metal levels as support for the marine disposal option. It is not known what the chronic, long-term effects of heavy metals or turbidities are. There may also be hidden costs such as reduced growth or reproduction. Animals may show temporary adaptation, but increases beyond these levels, or for extended periods of time may exceed their tolerances. Should the worst happen, salmon could avoid their regular migration routes and avoid the mining area.
I quote now from the West Coast Environmental Law Association:
The Alice Arm Tailings Deposit Regulations seem to run contrary to the over-all intent of the Fisheries Act, which allows exemptions only under extenuating circumstances, and only when minimum impact on fisheries resources has been clearly established.
We in Canada are not without experience in these matters. Just south of the present proposal is the Rupert Inlet operation of Utah Mines Limited which predicted that tailings would remain below 100 metres and settle in the deeper portions. I quote from an abstract regarding that particular operation:
Present studies have shown that the waste discharge from the copper mine has resulted in the anticipated obliterative effect on the deep benthos and an unpredicted widespread deposition of tailings which has affected the shallower, highly productive regions of the system.
Based on that experience, which is still occurring today, where the effluent is now several hundreds of miles out to sea and having a very serious and unknown impact on the fisheries resource, both the commercial and sport and food fishery, the government should call for a full public inquiry into the situation in Alice Arm.
In my view the Minister of Fisheries and Oceans should definitely hang his head in this House. The cost to the commercial fisheries is documented as being in the millions of dollars. The cost to the Nishga native people in that area is death. The company will save $23 million and the Liberal party will receive full credit, along with the Amax Corporation, but at enormous public cost.
Having dealt with just one particularly acute pollution occurrence in this country, I would like to move on to a second area in which the Minister of Fisheries and Oceans is not upholding his constitutional requirements, the Kemano completion project which began in the 1950s when the government of British Columbia gave to the Aluminum Company of Canada special water rights in northern B.C. Alcan constructed a dam on the Upper Nechako system backing up a double chain of lakes and rivers through the top of Tweedsmuir Park, flooding 925 square miles of land, now called the Nechako Reservoir.
This water was diverted from the Fraser River system, one of the largest salmon spawning rivers in the world, through a 16-kilometre tunnel to an underground power house at Kemano and it takes Fraser River water completely out of that system and pumps it through a tunnel directly into another area of the Pacific Ocean. The Kemano Completion Project intends to virtually shut down the Skins Lake spillway blocking almost all the water released into the Nechako River.
There is also the plan to dam the Nanika River which would flood Kitprice Lake and Nanika Lake, reversing the flow away from the Morice-Bulkley-Skeena system and into the Nechako Reservoir and back again to Kemano and another area of the Pacific. So we see the water rights given by the B.C. government allowing water to be taken from the Fraser system, which is crucially required there now because of pollution and low water, and from the Skeena system, being dumped in a different way by reversing flows into another area of the Pacific.
Alcan presently has two-thirds of the Nechako flows which has reduced the flows at, for example, Fort Fraser by 97 per cent, Vanderhoof by 83 per cent, and Prince George by 40 per cent. The new proposal would have a direct impact on the 1,500 native people on the Bulkley and Skeena systems and they would be directly and negatively impacted by the completion proposal. Last year's fisheries department and International Pacific Salmon Commission's study indicated that damage to salmon stocks would range from somewhere between $88 million and $372 million if Alcan is allowed to go ahead with this proposal. Definitely we are not talking about small peanuts, but from the responses we have received from the Minister of Fisheries it certainly seems that way.
In my view, a full public inquiry is required on this issue as well because mitigation and compensation, something which was espoused both by the previous Conservative government and the present Liberal government, really do little more than look at the impact on the value of salmon. It is a far more complex question when we are talking about flows going into the northern Pacific and down the Fraser River in terms of the impact on everyone in every community all the way down.
For example, this past summer Alcan refused, on the request of the Minister of Fisheries, to raise the levels of the Nechako River as requested for the safety of the in-coming spawning stocks. I think it is important that we question the motivation of a corporation when it refuses to raise the water level for the protection of a resource that has an equal right to be in operation. We must closely scrutinize what the Minister of Fisheries and the Minister of the Environment (Mr. Roberts) have done, and ask why they have not called for a full public inquiry.
In my view, the whole thing comes back to a very similar situation with regard to the Amax question where there seems to be a very close corporate tie between certain members of cabinet and various corporations. To date, there has always been more than enough electrical capacity for expanded smelter activity in the Kitimat area. Since 1950 approximately one third of the power generated has been sold into the general
October 27, 1980

B.C. hydro grid, and more aluminum production could also be achieved by the conservation of the electricity used in the present smelters by modernizing the pot lines,
Alcan is saying that it wants to produce more aluminum, and it can do it now without going ahead with this other flooding project and the siphoning off of water from another system. The option is there, but it has never gone ahead with that option. I think that it is important that those ministers, and those members in public life who are responsible for the interests of the public, stand up for once and help to preserve an industry which is seriously faltering in Canada.
Ten per cent of the salmon stocks in British Columbia are impacted by Kemano I project and Kemano II project. The minister has the power to modify and prevent construction of the project and, particularly, he has the right to call a full public inquiry into the issue, something which the minister hopscotched around over the past number of years. The 1950 agreement made between Alcan and the government of British Columbia can be readily modified. It was brought in and passed by the B.C. provincial cabinet and can be changed by either an act of the B.C. cabinet or by the provincial legislature. Although I do not think there are many, the Liberals and the Socreds in this particular situation are clearly in cahoots with Alcan on this issue.
In concluding, who within the government stands up for the commercial, native and sport fisheries in this country? Certainly, in my view and in the view of many fishermen in this country, it is not the present Minister of Fisheries. The list grows day by day. The previous speaker touched on the Ungava Bay situation, a very important issue with regard to the giving out of licences when there is a scientific study going on. It is certainly not in the interests of the Inuit with regard to the shrimp fishery. The list grows day by day. There is Arvik in the Arctic, Amax on the B.C. coast, Alcan on the Fraser and Skeena, Riley Creek, the English-Wabigoon pollution, the Great Lakes, the maritimes, and on it goes. All these failures, in my view, are results of bankrupt policies which come from that side of the House, of putting corporate brownie points ahead of public interest in our fish.

speakeroldname: Mr. George Henderson (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Fisheries and Oceans):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Fisheries and Oceans
subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S O. 58-ALLEGED FAILURE TO SUPPORT FISHING INDUSTRY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the motion before the House today makes me wonder whether the opposition has any knowledge of the real state of Canada's fisheries. To listen to the hon. member for Nanaimo-Alberni (Mr. Miller), you would think we were on the brink of disaster. Well, Mr. Speaker, I want to take the few minutes available to me to set the record straight. I want to tell the House that, while the fisheries are not without problems, their general state is very healthy, and the industry is a vibrant and valuable net contributor to the national economy.
Members opposite may be interested to know that the fisheries last year contributed something in the order of $1 billion to our balance of payments. We have become the biggest exporter in the world, in terms of the value of our fish
Fishing Industry
products. In fact we earned some $1.3 billion from exports of fish and seafood last year. An equally significant statistic is that the landed value of all Canadian fisheries was more than $873 million in 1979, and that is money which helps to support the economies of hundreds of small towns and villages on both coasts.
But the statistics do not tell the whole story. There is a feeling of stability in the fisheries. Catches are more reliable, plant work is steadier and stretches out over more of the year. There is growth in fishermen's organizations, as they gain status in their own communities and take a more direct role in the management of the industry from which they earn their livelihood. No longer is the fishery regarded as the employer of last resort.
The problems and opportunities of Canada's fisheries are certainly different from what they were only five or ten years ago. Throughout the 1970s the problems were problems of quantity. There simply was not enough fish to go around; the stocks were depressed, and a major rebuilding operation was necessary. That operation, which began after the disastrous experience of 1974, was given a major boost when Canada declared a 200-mile coastal fishing zone in 1977.
While I do not want to suggest that the 200-mile zone is the answer to all our problems, it has had a positive impact already. For example, Canadian fishermen's share of total fish catches taken from the Atlantic west of Greenland and north of Cape Cod ranged up to 37 per cent in the decade preceding 1977, but increased to 56 per cent last year.
In the waters within and immediately adjacent to the 200-mile zone, Canadian fishermen have made even more dramatic progress. Canadian catches in these waters increased from 895,000 metric tonnes in 1976 to 1.2 million tonnes in 1979, or an increase from 42 per cent to 73 per cent of the total taken by all fleets operating in the area. The principles of Canadian control and majority share of fishing within the zone have now been firmly established. Foreign fishing is permitted in the zone only after licence from the Canadian government, and is limited to stocks that are surplus to the needs of Canadian fishermen.
After Canada imposed the 200-mile limit there ensued a hue and cry for massive development, massive subsidies, massive fleet expansion. Fortunately this government resisted chasing pie in the sky-in the sea. This government's goal was, and continues to be, the encouragement of a solid industry which cannot only pay its own way but can contribute in a major way to the nation's economy. Nevertheless, we have to stop assuming that the fishery is some kind of gold mine. Instead, it is a garden, and if we care for it through sound management, it will last forever, helping to provide food for the world.
The policies of this government have added new co-ordination to the fishery, and a new degree of stability. We have avoided dictating too much development, by forcing people into boats or factories the government designs. Instead, we have tried to create a framework that sets the people free to work, free to develop their own future, in an industry that only six years ago faced bankruptcy and now can pay its own way.
4122

October 27, 1980
Fishing Industry
This government is establishing the co-ordination, the framework, the buffer margins of supply and profit that will let innovations take hold.
But nothing will go right unless, before all else, we protect the foundation and keep a stable supply of fish for a prosperous, dependable fleet. The fish are forever there but forever fragile, requiring careful management. We have begun building up a co-ordinated industry that can reach high. If, however, we fool around with the foundation, the rest will topple.
Because co-ordination has given us a fishery policy that works, I fear the tendencies that would again fragment fisheries management. Many provinces want more fisheries jurisdiction, not in the processing sector or the educational sector where they have every right and reason to do more, but in resource management, the issuing of licences, and the division of quotas.
What is the reasoning behind their demands? The Fathers of Confederation singled out the fishery resource as a special case, and the Fathers of Confederation were right. Herring, cod and even lobster move from province to province and country to country. You could catch all the southern gulf cod in the winter at Cape Breton and catch them all again that summer in the Gulf, if only you could catch the same fish twice. A Quebec salmon swims back to its river from Greenland past St. Pierre and Miquelon and four other provinces. A fish caught in a four-way tug of war is going to be a funny looking fish at the end.
Should provinces control the resource because they are more politically responsive to local needs? The federal system also has local members of Parliament. The federal government also has seven times the provincial number of fishery employees in Newfoundland and the maritimes, and the national government understands local demands and pressures. We also know that, after a point, the more politics, the less fish!
I think the reasons for the positions being put forward by some provincial governments come down to one. Their interest is because they can see fisheries is on the rise, they can see they need more jobs, and everyone has a natural tendency to think he could run the show better if he had the power. The trouble is, a single province can never really have final power. It is impossible to divide up a migratory common property resource in a satisfactory way, in such a limited area, and among so many interests.
Some may say we can have it both ways-provincial jurisdiction over fishing, various committees to co-ordinate matters, and the federal government to deal with research and international negotiations. Some hold up the regional councils in the United States as an example. But the regional councils have great difficulties in regulating fisheries, as we have learned on Georges Bank, and they would have even greater difficulties if their coast had huge internal multiprovincial pools like the Bay of Fundy and the Gulf of St. Lawrence.
I want to turn now to an issue which is one of the most urgent and important aspects of fisheries development, and that is licensing. The Minister of Fisheries and Oceans (Mr. LeBlanc) recently announced that his department's process of consultation with fishermen, processors and others in the industry, has been pretty well concluded, and that steps are now under way to implement a new licensing policy on the east coast. I want to welcome this initiative, and to urge members opposite to give the proposals their thoughtful consideration and support.
I should explain that the first move toward a new licensing policy was taken in late 1978, when the Minister of Fisheries and Oceans initiated a thorough review of prevailing conditions. Officials of the department held two rounds of consultations with fishermen during the winter of 1978-79, and the findings and recommendations of that study came to be known as the Levelton report. After that report was made public in June, 1979, another round of consultations was held with fishermen and other representatives of the industry, to assess their reactions and opinions. A broad outline of the government's proposals has already been referred to today by the Minister of State for Multiculturalism (Mr. Fleming).
Over all, the new system should give fishermen a more direct voice in matters having to do with licensing, and make the whole regime more equitable. I know that all hon. members would want to join me in encouraging the Minister of Fisheries and Oceans to continue his progress in implementing such a system.
Licences are necessary in the fishery in the same manner as such controls are necessary in other industries, Mr. Speaker. But we should never forget that, like any other resource based industry-mining, forestry, you name it-the fishery is subject to limits. It is an industry based on a finite resource. We tend to understand that about other resource industries. For example, nobody in his right mind would send 50 loggers into a forestry project if only 25 were required, or send 100 miners into a mine that should employ only 50. The same sort of respect for reality needs to be practised in the fishery. And the reality is that there is a good living to be made, but by a finite number of people.
This government's belief in and support of the fishing industry are manifested in many ways, Mr. Speaker. 1 have already provided the House with some statistics that show Canada's success in the export markets of the world. Our fishery enjoys a high reputation for the quality of its products. But we have to acknowledge that some parts of the industry could do a better job to maintain the consistency of quality. It is for this reason that the government this summer launched a major program to help the industry establish consistently high quality standards. The purpose of this program is to help those engaged in the fishery get more dollars for every pound of fish caught and, at the same time, ensure the consumer of a nutritious and delicious product.
The government's program to adopt new quality requirements has been developed in consultation with the industry. It will include the following main elements: a process of inspecting vessels and certifying them as properly equipped to pre-
October 27, 1980

serve the quality of fish; an improvement in handling practices on board vessels; the establishment of a system for grading the quality of fish landed; the setting of quality standards for the unloading, handling and transport of fish ashore; the introduction of rigorous quality control programs in fish processing plants; and the introduction of equally demanding standards for final products.
I also want to take this opportunity to welcome the announcement by the Minister of Fisheries and Oceans to create a new separate management region for the fishery in the Gulf of St. Lawrence. This arrangement will provide a co-ordinated focus for management of the fisheries in this area which is, after all, one ecological complex. It makes sense to have a single administration of a resource in which fishermen from five provinces participate.
The new management arrangement, as it has been outlined by the minister, will provide more affective, consistent policy and directional guidance, and help to promote increased cooperation between government and industry. The problems and priorities of the Gulf are often different from those experienced along the Atlantic offshore, so that the new region will be better equipped to meet these concerns.
When one realizes that more than 12,500 fishermen from all five eastern provinces participate in the Gulf fishery, and that the landed value of the main species last year was more than $70 million, we get some idea of the importance of this area to the economy of eastern Canada. Of the 100 processing plants surrounding the Gulf, 17 are operated by co-operatives, and 25 are operated as family businesses. Of the remaining 58, some 17 are branch plant operations of firms whose principal fish processing operations are located outside the Gulf area. Only 13 of the plants are supplied, in part, by company-owned vessels and well over 90 per cent of the raw material is supplied by fishermen who own their own vessels.
Up to 7,400 people find seasonal employment in the Gulf groundfish processing industry. Of these, 2,100 are employed in Newfoundland, 200 on the north shore of the Gulf, and 5,100 in the southwest area of the Gulf. Through the creation of the new management region, more attention can be given to ways of making the groundfishery in the Gulf more competitive by cost-reducing techniques, product development, diversification, market development and extension.
Details of the new region, such as its precise boundaries, the location of the headquarters, and the resources required, have not yet been determined. 1 am sure all members will be interested in this information when it becomes available.
There are those in the industry who argue that Canada needs more freezer-trawlers, and even factory freezer-trawlers. To those I would point out that, taken together, the inshore and nearshore fleet of independently-owned vessels are the backbone of our fishing industry. These boats far exceed the offshore fleet in value of landings, number of boats, and number of fishermen. They are the basic source of life of the hundreds of fishing communities in whose name this government negotiated the 200-mile limit. When the question is asked for whom the fishery is being developed, we have to
Fishing Industry
think in the first instance of the independent, inshore and nearshore fishermen.
The allocation of the fishery resource has been subject to a tug-of-war for a long time, but care must be taken to avoid parcelling out fish on the basis of "to the strongest, the spoils" Some would defend the rights of large vessels owned by large companies to roam to the very shore, on the basis of "rugged individualism"; but who is a more rugged individual than the small fisherman, owning his own boat, and counting on a fair chance at the nearby fish?
Canada argued before the world for the 200-mile zone, not so a few major companies could earn more dividends, but in the name of the small coastal communities. The shareholders of large corporations deserve their fair returns. The allocating of fish must be done for a variety of reasons, not just because it is economical, but also for community survival, for the preservation of a way of life, for the needs of the marketplace, for the reasonable well-being of fishermen and plant workers, and so on.
We need not worship the idea of a 12-month trawler fishery above all. Nor for that matter need we worship inshore fishery claims to exclusiveness, in a case where allowing only an inshore fishery might mean just six weeks work and nine months of unemployment insurance. Common sense reference points are required in establishing quotas and allocating fish between fleets.
1 was pleased the Minister of Fisheries and Oceans convened a seminar this year with representatives of the fishing industry and the provincial governments of the Atlantic region to discuss Gulf of St. Lawrence groundfish. Such meetings have given fishermen, processors and the provincial governments an opportunity to participate in both short and long-range planning for a variety of fisheries. I understand that additional seminars will be held this fall and winter, and I think the minister should be congratulated for this practice of involving the industry representatives.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am delighted to participate in this debate this afternoon and to compliment my colleague, the hon. member for Nanaimo-Alberni (Mr. Miller). He has roundly and soundly condemned the government for their negligence in dealing with the fisheries of Canada's Atlantic coast, the west coast and the inland waters as well. I am afraid my remarks will not be quite as complimentary as those made by the previous speaker, the hon. member for Egmont (Mr. Henderson).
What we have seen is 12 years of mismanagement of the fisheries of Canada, aside from a short nine-month period last year when certain initiatives were taken to sort out some of this mess. If hon. members opposite deny the validity of what 1 just said, perhaps they would be enlightened if I were to read the first sentence of a letter we recently received from the present Minister of Fisheries and Oceans (Mr. LeBlanc). This letter was sent to members of Parliament who represent fishing communities, on October 10, 1980. The first sentence of the letter reads as follows:
As you know, there are serious problems facing the Pacific coast commercial salmon fishery which call for immediate action as well as longer term solutions. To assist me in deciding the best course of action, I recently asked Dr. Peter Pearse and Mr. Fern Doucet to meet with representatives of the provincial government and the Pacific fishing sector in order to examine the principal problems-
What we read is an admission by the present Minister of Fisheries and Oceans that there are serious problems in our Pacific coast fishery, resulting from years of mismanagement and neglect. As my colleague from Malpeque pointed out, the previous Progressive Conservative minister, the hon. member for St. John's East (Mr. McGrath), initiated as his first act of office, a white paper policy review. Many people in the Department of Fisheries were involved and considerable funds were spent in preparing a new direction for Canada's fishery development in the eighties. For some reason this whole initiative has now been buried. The present minister will not report to this House on the findings of that major policy review which was conducted last year.
It was also an initiative of the previous Conservative government that the Sinclair and Levelton licensing reports were to have been reviewed by the standing committee in consultation with fishermen's groups. The present minister has done very little with regard to adopting, enacting or moving on the recommendations of Drs. Sinclair and Levelton.
The management initiatives that were taken during 1979 were very necessary and long overdue; on both coasts, for example, the establishment of a policy on freezer trawlers, the imposition of a moratorium on sea-licensed vessels on the west coast. The minister will know that, on the verge of our defeat
October 27, 1980

in this House last December, there were a number of very strident and some difficult policy announcements prepared, to be made, about which many of the Conservative minister's colleagues felt uncomfortable. However, they were necessary initiatives. The present minister has completely abdicated on them.
The previous minister also initiated a major review of the Freshwater Fish Marketing Corporation which has been managing, developing and burgeoning into a vertically integrated Crown corporation, dominating the fishery from lakeside to the export of the product. The management practices of that corporation are highly questionable. The previous minister, the hon. member for St. John's East, initiated an in-depth study of that Crown corporation. The findings of that study were to have been presented in April at a meeting of fisheries ministers of the affected provinces. To date we have not heard anything from the present minister.
I commend the present Minister of Fisheries and Oceans on finally admitting that there is a problem with regard to the west coast fishery in particular, and initiating steps for a solution of that problem. He returned from vacation at the end of August and immediately initiated a study by Messrs. Pearse and Doucet, two gentlemen who are going to solve all of the problems for him.
We commend the initiative reflected in that study. However, we wonder what was happening the previous seven months of that minister's reincarnation. We now see that international negotiations are beginning to bear fruit. The minister was kind enough a couple of weeks ago to invite input and opinions from members on this side of the House, but not until the Pearse-Doucet study had been under way for some six or seven weeks. We were given 48 hours to respond before he was off to a meeting in British Columbia where he would reflect on our recommendations and those of others in meeting the representatives of the west coast industry.
We are also grateful that in recent weeks we learned that the budget for managing the Pacific coast fishery was increased by an additional $3 million on a $60 million budget and that additional funding will be directed toward increasing enforcement personnel in particular. We appreciate that.
I must repeat that it is ludicrous for a minister who was in office since 1974, and granted the opportunity of a brief sabbatical leave, to take seven months to get himself moving again on his return to office. It has been a disappointment to those on this side that he has taken so long in getting to work on the serious problems which face the west coast fisheries industry at least.
The motion put by the hon. member for Nanaimo-Alberni is in four parts. The first two parts deal with international negotiations and the question of high interest rates and the difficulties that poses for fishermen. I will touch on that rather quickly. 1 really want to deal for most of my talk with the third and fourth parts of the motion which question the management policies of the present government and the minister in his previous incarnation. As well, I want to deal with the lack of
Fishing Industry
adequate enforcement and protection of the habitat of the fishery.
First, with regard to international negotiations, meetings between the Canadian and United States negotiating teams have been far too infrequent. The approach to the problems of halibut and albacore tuna and the salmon interception, particularly affecting the Fraser River, has been piecemeal and reactionary to crises, sort of at the eleventh hour. There has been far too much of this last minute firefighting. For example, we knew in June and July there was a proposal which would have staved a crisis regarding albacore tuna which had been received by the minister and his department. They did nothing with that proposal until the U.S. tuna boats were already en route pursuing the albacore tuna once again into Canadian waters. The only way we avoided having once again to take U.S. fishermen into custody, as the previous minister did a year ago, was to come up with a last minute fix which many fishermen on the west coast feel was a sell out of our interests. It weakened our hand in negotiating with some of the other important concessions, particularly with regard to Fraser River salmon.
A great concern of mine with regard to international negotiations arises from the fact that members of Parliament and U.S. senators are not part of the process and are not even welcome at these negotiating sessions. I believe that slows down the process. It means that after an agreement is reached and signed as a tentative accord, it then has to be subjected to the real world of political pressures, as we saw with the east coast treaty, to the extent that all of that work may have been for naught because the political spokesmen do not fully understand the issues and the complexities behind the negotiations. I was disappointed when I asked in June to be permitted to observe the west coast negotiations which were held in Vancouver. The department, essentially, said no, my presence would not be welcomed there, although members of the fishing industry, members of the canning companies and of the various fishing organizations were welcomed, but it was not appropriate for a member of Parliament to be present. I really question that decision because I think that if we are going to make progress in these talks we must stop sitting back, as Canada usually does, and stop waiting for our American friends to put their cards on the table. We have to seize the initiative and we have to be realistic when it comes to the political factors which enter into these decisions. While we sit back on our complacent butts, the United States goes ahead and does as it wishes.
Although I am pleased to hear today that a tentative agreement is being struck for the west coast salmon interception problem, I am afraid that if we read this agreement carefully we will realize that all future increases of enhanced salmon stocks on the Fraser River will be given to Canada but we will have to pay the shot for enhancing them. That is an easy commitment for the Americans to make if there are no effective means of control to ensure that we do indeed reap the benefits of that enhanced stock.

October 27, 1980
Fishing Industry
1 will be running short of time, Mr. Speaker, so 1 will comment quickly on the interest rate matter. The NDP motion implies that the government can regulate interest rates. I suggest that the interest rate problem is a consequence of Canada's very unhealthy economy and our growing, continuing and deepening vulnerability to the deficits that this government is incurring. But the government does have the opportunity, through the Federal Business Development Bank and the Fisheries Improvement Loans Act, to assist fishermen. In particular, this House would, when we revised the Fisheries Improvement Loans Act in June, have demanded that the chartered banks which lend money to fishermen, guarantee an interest rate for at least a five-year term, because at present I have many constituents who come to me saying, "We have a loan with the Federal Business Development Bank at 7 per cent, 8 per cent or 9 per cent. It is expiring and suddenly they want 17 per cent".
I should like to tell you, Mr. Speaker, what the impact of that is on a couple of fishermen who happen to have a loan of a quarter of a million dollars on a seine boat, for example. The impact of an interest rate rising from 9 per cent or 10 per cent to 17 per cent would be in the order of $25,000 in one year. We have to realize that those two fishermen, who are employing a crew, meeting all their expenses and having to contend with dwindling stock levels, are taking home between $8,000 to $15,000 or perhaps $18,000 a year, and suddenly they are hit with an additional $25,000 a year. How will they pay it? They will have to contend with bankruptcy in many cases.
I think there are initiatives which the government can take. The small business development bonds which were proposed in our budget are effective means of bringing down interest rates. They should be extended to the fishery sector. There is also the mechanism of tax credits whereby those who are investing in fishing vessels are allowed to deduct their interest expenses from income immediately before calculating taxable income.
As hon. members on the other side often point out, and as the minister is fond of saying, we have a problem in the west coast fishery of too many vessels chasing too few fish. We have an excess capacity of fishing vessels relative to the available stock level. I have to ask: who created this problem? Why did it come to this point in 1980 when we have far too many vessels and, in particular, when we have five or six hundred of the largest vessels, the seine vessels, which have accumulated tonnages, to some extent, on the basis of vessels which were sold under the federally-sponsored buy-back program in the 1970s? Now we have the ludicrous situation where these large seine vessels are abie to fish a few hours a week in the summer if they are lucky, whereas the troll fleet is out fishing seven days a week and for a considerably longer period of time.
We have so much fishing power concentrated in this fleet of large seine vessels that they are only allowed to fish a few hours a week, and they are still economically viable on that basis. They may not be attractive in terms of employing large numbers of people, but the owners argue that they are the best return on investment capital. Perhaps we cannot argue with
that if we believe that they are husbanding the resource as effectively as the trawlers and the gillnet vessels do.
We have a number of other problems with the west coast fishery. We have the problem of an inadequate emphasis on the salmon enhancement program, especially with respect to the more choice natural stocks of sockeye, Chinook and such species running into the Fraser River system. We are putting a lot of effort into enhancing the cheaper varieties of salmon and none at all into the salmon enhancement facilities which should be built and under way on the Fraser River system.
We have a situation where there is inadequate enforcement, and only $4 million of the west coast fisheries budget, out of some $50 million, is devoted to provision of salaries for enforcement personnel numbering around 115 officers on the whole of the British Columbia coast.
There is too much waste of juvenile fish being thrown overside or being caught as a by-catch or of other species which a fisherman is not allowed to fish which is being caught be accident and thrown overboard because he is not allowed to take it to dockside. One wonders if we are really being wise in encouraging this waste by requiring that fishermen not bring to shore fish which they should not have caught in the first place. One wonders if it might not be much better to require that they not be allowed to throw fish overboard and that they account for their actions when they get to shore if they were fishing out of their zone, in an area where they should not have been. The onus would then be on the fisherman to explain why that happened.
We have a serious problem with poaching and the illegal selling of fish in the lower Fraser Valley in particular, and the ministry seems to be doing very little about that.
With regard to solutions, Mr. Speaker, there are two classes of solutions to the problem of too many vessels chasing too few fish. The minister knows very well that one type of solution has to do with conservation, that is to say, we have to find ways to stop over-Fishing. The other solution is to enhance what we have, to increase the supply of Fish. On the conservation side, it is, I believe, important that we establish a nominal allocation of the available catch among the three sectors of the salmon fleet and, for want of a better number, I would say that perhaps it should be allocated one-third each way. We must allocate between the two sectors of the herring-roe fishery, the seine and the gillnet fishermen who have been sharing that resource in recent years relatively equally.
To impose an allocation scheme requires a political decision, and I suggest that the present minister must show the courage necessary to take that political decision and tell each sector of the industry that they will fish with one gear type and that this will be allocated in accordance with recent historical precedent. He should tell them that upon completion of each fishing year the department would record the value of catches by these various gear types and plan their management policies for the next year in order to ensure that the allocation is properly met by imposing restrictions and regulations on the size of hooks, whether or not they should be barbless, the net size, and other area restrictions. The department has the power
October 27, 1980

to adjust the relative catch of the various types of gear in order to maintain a fair sharing of the resource among the various gear types.
If I have another moment or two, Mr. Speaker, I should like to say that it seems to me, if you have a formula for allocating the catch between the gear types, if there is a question of too much fishing power, we should leave it to the investors in those various gear types to decide whether they want to buy out some of their competitors. We should look at the possibility of a voluntary or self-operated buy-back program. If we have 500 of the same vessels and if those owners feel they are not getting enough action individually, perhaps they should pay a portion each year on their licence fee in order to fund the buy-back program. The same boat owners could fund their own buy-back program, and the gillnetters and trollers could do likewise. This would enable the initiative to be placed upon the investors in these vessels to decide for themselves whether they are willing to contend with excess competition, being subject to a specific quota of fish, or whether they want indeed to reduce the number of vessels in their sector of the industry.
On the enhancement side-and I see I do not have any additional time left-I just want to say that we must put much greater emphasis on enhancing the salmon stocks in the Fraser River system. We cannot wait until our friends across the way resolve the problem with the Americans. We have to invest in those important hatchery and enhancement facilities in the Fraser system now if we are going to realize a benefit from them by the end of this decade. So, we must do that. We must finance the enhancement projects, and I believe the fishermen are prepared to assist in financing those projects through some form of cash royalty if it goes into a dedicated fund specifically earmarked for SEP projects and if they have representation on a board of trustees which administers that fund.
Thank you for waiting for an extra moment, Mr. Speaker. I will take my seat.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S O. 58-ALLEGED FAILURE TO SUPPORT FISHING INDUSTRY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the motion presented today is very important, and I would like to elaborate on some of the remarks made by my colleagues, the hon. member for Nanaimo-Alberni (Mr. Miller) and the hon. member for Skeena (Mr. Fulton), and also to acknowledge the significant contribution made by other hon. members on this side of the House who have spoken.
Some of the things which disturbed me in this afternoon's debate were the statements by the present Parliament Secretary to the Minister of Fisheries and Oceans (Mr. Henderson) and those by the previous one. What disturbed me about their comments was the implication that basically all is well in the fishing industry and that things are generally improving. The only conclusion I can draw is that the comments of somebody from downtown Toronto commenting on the fishing industry may be a little distorted, and although such a person may not have the age and experience to have seen the development of the west coast industry or the east coast industry and the way things have progressed over the years, I urge him to consider
Fishing Industry
that the unanimous opinion of most of the people involved, especially in this House, is that it is in very serious jeopardy on the west coast.
The present parliamentary secretary had the fortunate experience of being able to travel to my riding and to take a few of the more choice species on the hook. I have certainly enjoyed the experience and acquired some fairly good insights, but obviously the hon. member must need another trip out there. I encourage him to return and to look more deeply into what appears to be a very serious problem which may not be apparent at first blush.
In my presentation today I would like to deal specifically with things which affect my riding. Some of the comments I have made before, but they could be reinforced here. In my riding there are two basic industries, fishing and forestry. Forestry, of course, is the prime one, but the fishing industry is vitally important to those people who live in small communities. Under the present management practices of the Department of Fisheries and Oceans, what has been happening on the west coast is that many small communities are in very serious jeopardy. The only thing many of the Indian communities have had to depend on over the years is forestry, and over the years they have been deprived of access to the forest resource. Unfortunately the only other asset is fishing, and that is being constantly curtailed, which I suggest places them in difficult straits.
In many of those communities we see unemployment rates which hinge around 75 per cent, and in an especially poor season when the canneries are not working and employment is restricted, Indian access to the resource generally and to licences, vessels and processing is minimal, and the picture looks very bleak. I suggest to the present parliamentary secretary that in fact that industry is in a very difficult situation in relation to some consideration of its historic appearance. Some people are doing well, but a very large number are doing poorly under the present system, and the prognosis is very grim.
I would like to deal with four aspects of the problem as I see it, and they deal basically with the management question, the environment question, the enhancement of the Pacific coast species, and the allocation of catch.
First, with regard to the environment, both of my colleagues, the hon. member for Nanaimo-Alberni and the hon. member for Skeena, have outlined their very serious concerns, but in my riding I face a number of serious concerns, as do the fishermen there. For example, there are large areas on the west coast of British Columbia, on Vancouver Island, and on the Queen Charlottes which are very rich in coal, and we are going to see a tremendous resource conflict.
We have the prospect of open-pit coal mining. Studies have been undertaken by the Department of the Environment and the Department of Fisheries and Oceans which say that this open-pit coal mining can go ahead. Proposals are already in. Second-stage studies are completed, and it looks as if we will be having open-pit coal mines. In the future, as we make the transition from oil and gas, we will see a tremendous influx of

October 27, 1980
Fishing Industry
open-pit coal mines. From my listening at public meetings and in discussions with officials in the department I have learned that we have not even begun to consider the drastic consequences for our fishing resources. As a matter of fact, just southwest of Campbell River an open-pit coal mine will be built in the headwaters to one of the major show hatcheries at Quinsam. I have never heard of such a contradiction; nevertheless, processing and an open-pit coal mine will be allowed. There really is no appreciation of what is going to happen there.
However, that is only the beginning. There will be numerous attempts to develop that coal resource as the pressure on us increases. What will happen is that coal will go in and fisheries will go out.
Another contradiction in developing those open-pit coal mines is that the department and other individuals who are developing them are trying to reassure us that the department has sufficient monitoring and enforcement capabilities to see that those coal developers follow the guidelines laid down, yet we wind up with enforcement people telling us that they do not have the person-years, the budget nor the time to deal with all the problems in the fisheries. The hon. member for Richmond-South Delta (Mr. Siddon) mentioned a $3 million increase in the enforcement section of the budget. That will not scratch the surface when we consider the tremendous development which will be going on.
There are numerous examples. We have the Amax situation and the pending situation at Campbell River. Mining is only one aspect of it, but the situation will become very serious in the future, and we are completely unprepared to meet what I feel will be the total destruction of our fish-rearing habitat as a result.
The forest industry, the number one industry in British Columbia, has been the number one competitor for land use as between fisheries and forestry, and essentially the predominant industry under provincial control is basically eroding the available habitat for fish rearing.
In the past loggers have come in and logged out the valley bottoms where the quick, cheap timber is available. Erosion and destruction of streams for spawning and juvenile fish rearing has been total. We wind up with flooding. Once the spawning species have gone up, the soil can no longer hold moisture and when there are heavy rains, they simply flush the system out totally. If we head up through the area around Bella Coola, we find that where there once were spawning streams we now just have conduits which run water down, and there is no spawning capability.
The unregulated forest industry has gone a long way in the past toward destroying the habitat on which this resource is based. The Kimsquit Valley will be logged out. In that area chums and a variety of other species are raised. We saw what happened at Riley Creek, and until that conflict is resolved satisfactorily and until the department has the capability of enforcing habitat protection, with laws which are essentially on the books, we will not find that our habitat will be
preserved, and the resource will eventually be eroded out from underneath us.
Also with regard to the environment, as we come down the coast of British Columbia and down Vancouver Island, we find that the demand for land use in every estuary is for industrial purposes, for the dumping of municipal sewage or for land fill. Essentially we are giving up an area which is probably far more productive in its food raising capability than any farmland in British Columbia. I would point to the Comox estuary where there have been landfill projects. It was felt that the best place to build a sewage lagoon was right in the middle of that valuable productive estuary. Industries in that particular valley locate right smack in the middle of the estuary. They do not locate in other areas somewhat farther away where it might be slightly more difficult for them to develop. Every single development, every piece of landfill poured in there and every piece of sewage poured in there destroys the capability to raise fish. We are witnessing the destruction of the resource.
I should like to turn to the Campbell River estuary. The municipality of Campbell River appealed to the federal government for assistance in relocating industry, stopping further encroachment and trying to reverse some of the tremendous damage which has been done. We are now in the process of a new project in the Comox estuary which will dump more raw sewage. Basically we need a commitment on the part of the Department of Fisheries and Oceans and on the part of the provincial government of British Columbia to move quickly to preserve its extremely valuable fish rearing and food raising capabilities. But I do not see any action. I just see continuous and serious erosion in such areas along the entire coast.
Turning to the Fraser River, in the area in which I was born and raised, I had quite a shock the other day. On various occasions I have walked a good piece of that river from Mission to its mouth on both sides. I was under the impression that it was still in the state it was when I was much younger. The trip up that river in a fish boat the other day scared me, and I say that seriously. Not only is there a tremendous load and discharge of sewage, chemical wastes, poisons of all sorts and varieties into it, but there seems to be a structural change in that river designed to get rid of marshes and fishery habitat competing for land use in its estuary and, I guess, the associated fish-supporting aspects of that river. It has been mentioned before, but 1 should like to add my voice to it: with the destruction of that river will probably come the destruction of the fishing industry in the province of British Columbia. That river is in such a serious state right now that a parliamentary task force should be set up to study what is taking place.
The provincial government of British Columbia seems committed to asserting its constitutional authority. That is probably the only explanation we could give for some of the more bizarre aspects of its policymaking. It had the recent misfortune of one of the ministers in charge of lands coming out to my riding and stating that they were declaring a moratorium on booming grounds in Baynes Sound, an area located along
October 27, 1980

the shoreline of my riding. They were declaring a moratorium after they had let MacMillan Bloedel build one more big booming ground. The purpose of the press release was to suggest that the moratorium would apply after this big booming ground had been completed. Bark drops and decays and hydrogen sulphide develop and poison the water so that fish and fry can no longer use it and those areas stay poisoned for roughly 25 years. There are areas in the Comox estuary where these same logging companies have deposited a layer of bark and decaying material in which there is no oxygen and a substantial amount of hydrogen sulphide; no fish are capable of living in such waters. I suggest to the parliamentary secretary-and 1 would suggest it to the minister if he were here- that action on environmental issues associated with the fisheries would bear tremendous benefits, especially assertive action which would protect the base upon which the entire industry is structured. This is extremely important, and I suggest the minister and the government of the country have been negligent in defending that aspect.
We desperately need a coast-line management act to protect foreshore, estuary and habitat. There is not much point in continuing discussion of the Kemano project after the hon. member for Skeena has dealt with it but I should like to suggest one further aspect. The Kemano project is a conflict in resources; electricity has become more valuable than fish. When we look at its location, it is on the central coast of British Columbia. Some of the streams will eventually back up, ensuring a decrease in fishing, fish habitat and fishery capabilities on the central coast of British Columbia. It will be one further erosion of the capacity of people in that area to earn a living, as well as constituting an environmental disaster. Basically we are suffering from a tremendous degree of negligence in terms of preserving the environment upon which the west coast fishing industry relies. When we lose this environment-and we are continuing to lose it at a faster and faster rate-then we will not have to worry about buy-back programs, overcapitalization, a salmon enhancement program, reserving manpower or budgetary requirements, because we will have destroyed the capability to support that industry. It is extremely important that this be recognized and acted upon.
I think the area of management has been covered pretty well today. We have looked at the question of research, enforcement, the licensing scheme, possibilities for the allocation of fish, overcapitalization and so on; we have talked about consultation and concentration. Some key topics were developed today in terms of their impact upon the west coast fishery, but I should like to add a few comments of my own. Research is extremely important. It does not show. The hon. member for Nanaimo-Alberni suggested that it is not a very glamorous aspect and that it takes a lot of input over a long period of time before benefits are developed. It does not show like a new hatchery or a new fishing vessel. But it is absolutely vital. If we cut back long-term research commitments, or if we cut
Fishing Industry
back on research at all, we will pay the price in the long run, because we will not be able to support the industry.
Other bizarre things seem to be happening there. Rather than budgeting or paying out of the budget for a planned research program, we now seem to be bargaining to get fishing vessel owners to undertake support programs for research, and we are paying them with a catch allocation. We seem to have grabbed the Japanese to come in and to research for us, because we are not willing to pay Canadian vessel owners to undertake some of that research. We are exchanging research undertakings for the right to catch fish. I suggest that is absolutely wrong. Since it is one of the pillars that support this very vital industry, we must plan our long-term research commitment and we must allocate the required resources. We should be supporting Canadian vessel owners and Canadian crews in undertaking that research, in developing the expertise within our own industry. Essentially we should be creating that employment and expertise here so that we can improve our own industry and not turn it back to the Japanese. Enough of it is controlled there already.
I would like to express my thoughts on enforcement, as well. We do not have enough fisheries officers. The government seems to be committed to cutbacks in staffing, in support services, in a whole variety of areas. There is a mentality which favours cutting back the civil service which provides these very vital services to the citizens of this country. It appears to me, though, that if we withdraw budget support for these essential programs we are really adopting on a penny wise and pound foolish approach. We should make a solid commitment to enforcement, provide expert fisheries personnel who can monitor these environmental problems, go after violators who degrade the natural habitat, and see to the enforcement of conservation program. Not only that, in the final analysis the government has got to back them up when they lay charges, when they say, for example, that a foreshore should not be paved in order to meet values which are less in the long term than the value of the fisheries. The government should be backing these people up. Without such backing, financial commitment and person-years, we might as well forget it because we will never really know what is developing and what is going wrong in that industry.
Enforcement is an extremely serious part of this process and we are not living up to our full commitment. With respect to the licensing scheme the two parliamentary secretaries who preceded me said it had come out better than sliced bread. Well, judging from the people I dealt with-this is probably the single largest file in my office-there are tremendous problems. People have been put out of the industry and lost their livelihood because of that licensing system.
