1 thank hon. members for giving me the opportunity to sum up. The licensing scheme has been a disaster, but 1 would like to move to the question of allocation, which was dealt with by the hon. member for Richmond-South Delta (Mr. Siddon), by the hon. member for Nanaimo-Alberni and the hon. member for Skeena. The allocation situation appears to be far more complicated. What will happen is this: we will reach a situation in which there will be allocating between sports fishermen, commercial fishermen and Indian communities. Many coastal Indian communities are absolutely dependent upon that resource. A commitment has to be made to the Indian people which will assure them of access to that resource so that they can support their communities at a financial or economic level which will allow them to lead what we consider to be a decent life. If we are to resolve unemployment and some of these financial problems and give a certain independence to those Indian communities, they must be considered in that allocation program. So when we are speaking of allocation we are not just talking about sports fishing or commercial fishing, we are not just talking about gear-type, we are talking as well about providing an allocation to a group in British Columbia whose only option, in many cases, because of the geographic location in which they find themselves is to resort to that resource.
With those remarks, Mr. Speaker, I thank hon. members and resume my seat.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S O. 58-ALLEGED FAILURE TO SUPPORT FISHING INDUSTRY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I certainly appreciate the opportunity to participate in this debate although 1 note it is an opposition day. In my opening remarks I would like to refer to the first part of the motion which says:
That this House condemns the government for its failure to support the Canadian fishing industry, as demonstrated
(a) by betraying the interests of Canadian fishermen in its international fisheries negotiations with the United States;
Before I deal with that particular topic I would like to clarify a few inconsistencies which I believe have become evident here today. I believe it was the hon. member for Malpeque (Mr. Gass) who made some comments in relation to the Atlantic Salmon Advisory Board. He indicated that the minister was not involved in the process, nor in the past was he in the habit of using this particular board. It is my understanding that this is incorrect. I am told that the minister has met with the chairman and vice-chairman of this board on numerous occasions and that he has asked several members of the board to undertake specific consultations regarding the possibility of reopening the fisheries in the areas where a ban was imposed-I believe this took place some time in 1972.
I understand that these consultations have now been completed and that the minister will soon be meeting with those concerned to hear their advice. Dealing with the wider aspect, I believe the minister is prepared to listen to these officials, as well as others, on all aspects of the Atlantic salmon management.
There were also a few comments made by the hon. member for Central Nova (Mr. MacKay) with regard to the policy
affecting freezer-trawlers and factory freezer-trawlers. The present government has not altered the previous government's policy of licensing vessels to fish underutilized species but otherwise of issuing no further groundfish licenses. And none have been issued. It is my understanding that only one holder of an underutilized species licence has acquired a vessel. Some have suggested that given the economics of fishing such species, the previous government may have given some people a licence to go bankrupt.
I think it would be useful to review the steps and events in our relationship with the United States over the past four years as they relate to fisheries. This review will indicate the efforts which have been made to protect the interests of fishermen on both our coasts. Canada and the United States each extended their fisheries jurisdiction to 200 miles in 1977-Canada on January 1, 1977, for both the Atlantic and Pacific coasts, and the U.S.A. on March 1, 1977. In the period preceding these extensions, negotiations had been initiated between the two countries to try to develop an agreement which would protect the interests of the fishermen of both countries when extensions of jurisdiction came into effect. These negotiations were under way when the Canadian extension came into force and Canada acted, at that time, to protect the negotiating process by passing an order in council to allow United States vessels to continue fishing in Canadian waters until a reciprocal fisheries agreement was completed. The assumption of the Canadian government at that time was that if negotiations for a reciprocal agreement were not completed by March 1, the date on which the U.S. extension would come into force, Canada would expect interim treatment of the same kind for Canadian fishermen until the negotiations were concluded.
As things worked out, an interim reciprocal fisheries agreement applicable to both east and west coasts was worked out. It was effective from February 14, 1977, to the end of the year. The first reciprocal agreement in the period following extensions of jurisdiction had two primary objectives. The first was to allow fishermen of both countries to continue their existing fishing patterns. The second objective was to avoid conflict or prejudice to legal claims in the boundary regions by ensuring that neither party would licence third countries to fish within the area of overlapping claims and providing for flag state enforcement by Canada and the United States, that is, within the area of overlapping claims Canadian laws would apply to, and be enforced against, only Canadian fishermen and the United States would take similar action with respect to United States vessels. This interim agreement was amended in 1978, subject to ratification by both countries. The amendments were designed to deal with problems which had developed under the fisheries agreement of 1977, particularly those involving troll fishing for salmon on the west coast. However, problems continued over the salmon troll fishery on the west coast while the 1978 agreement was being provisionally applied pending ratification.
Because of these difficulties, the Canadian government suspended provisional implementation of the agreement in June,
October 27, 1980

1978, and it was never ratified. The result of this suspension was that the U.S. fishermen were excluded from the Canadian fishing zone and Canadian fishermen were excluded from the U.S. fishing zone except for special arrangements for halibut fishing under the halibut fishing treaty on the west coast. Fishing by both countries continued, of course, in the areas of overlapping claims on both coasts.
The supsension of reciprocal fishing by the Canadian government in 1978 was a serious step taken with the full support of the Canadian fishing industry to protect Canadian interests. It had become obvious to both the government and the industry that the U.S. government was subject to powerful influences which were making it difficult or impossible for the United States to live up to its commitment to Canada. The suspension of reciprocal fishing at the initiative of the Canadian government avoided the creation of a situation where U.S. fishermen would be obtaining benefits in Canadian waters out of balance with the benefits Canadian fishermen were obtaining in U.S. waters.
The suspension also served notice to the United States that the Government of Canada would not let the interests of the Canadian fishing industry be eroded under pressure and that any agreement reached with the United States would have to be based on an equitable balancing of benefits and interests. Even though the reciprocal fishing agreement of 1978 never came into force, the arrangement between the two countries on how to handle fishing in the boundary areas was continued under, what I might call a gentleman's agreement.
The gentleman's agreement continued the same regime for the boundary areas as applied under the reciprocal agreements. That is, neither country would licence foreign fishing vessels to fish in the area of overlapping claims and there would be flag state enforcement by the United States and Canada. Canada and the United States now undertook an entirely new initiative to try to resolve both boundaries and fisheries on both coasts through the designation of special negotiators for this purpose, Ambassador Marcel Cadieux for Canada and Mr. Lloyd Cutler for the U.S.A.
I do not wish to dwell at length on the pros and cons of these complex negotiations. Suffice it to say that the negotiations for agreements on boundaries and fisheries on the west coast failed, but after a great deal of work by the special negotiators, the negotiating teams and the fishing industries of both sides, an agreement on the east coast was achieved, and signed on March 29, 1979.
The signing of the complex east coast fisheries agreement may be considered both a tribute to the negotiating teams and a reflection of the painstaking care by the negotiating teams to work out a fair balance between the fishing interests of both countries on a stock by stock and percentage point by percentage point basis.
First of all, the agreement refers the boundary issue to international adjudication. Next, and of overriding significance, the agreement provides for conservation of the fish stocks in the Georges Bank area for the periods both preceding and following the eventual settlement of the boundary by
Fishing Industry
establishing a fisheries commission to manage the stocks, and effective arbitration mechanisms to ensure that those stocks will not suffer from any failure to reach agreement within the commission.
Finally, the agreement provides an insurance policy for the fishermen of both countries. No matter where the boundary is placed as a result of the international adjudication, each country is given a fixed percentage entitlement from the total allowable catch limit to be set each year for each stock. This will provide stability for the fishermen of both countries. But the system also provides for a considerable degree of flexibility. The agreed percentage shares are subject to review every ten years, with reductions in shares possible for a variety of reasons. There are ceilings on the amount of the possible reductions for each decade, and a maximum ceiling to avoid the possibility that any group of fishermen would find itself totally excluded from a stock in which it has had a traditional interest.
The situation on the west coast has progressed somewhat differently. Given the impasse reached in the boundaries and fisheries negotiations, discussions between the two countries have focused on individual stocks and, indeed, individual problems.
The salmon interception negotiations have carried on, continuing along the lines developed since the negotiations began in the early 1970s. A full report on the meeting in Seattle last week, which I understand met with some success, is now in the process of being prepared.
Canadian halibut Fishermen continue to have access to U.S. waters off Alaska under arrangements worked out two years ago, which are to terminate on or about March 31, 1981. This was in exchange for allowing the U.S. fishermen access to groundfish off the Canadian Pacific coast. It is difficult to say at this time what is likely to happen to this area of reciprocity in 1981-82, but a major success for both countries is that we have kept the Halibut Commission in existence to provide an institutional framework for co-operation between the two countries on halibut conservation.
Finally, as hon. members know, we have had difficulties with the U.S.A. over albacore tuna in the Pacific coast. However, I believe we are well on the way toward a treaty which will provide substantial benefits to Canadian fishermen through access to U.S. ports to sell their tuna catches.
We should not, of course, overlook the fact that difficult issues lie ahead on the west coast. Boundaries remain to be settled, and we are still considerably short of a comprehensive framework to govern conservation and fisheries between Canada and the U.S.A. The difficulties we have had with the east coast agreement must inevitably give rise to misgivings about the possibilities, but the Government of Canada will continue to press for the adoption of a rational relationship with the U.S.A. on both our coasts so as to protect the interests of all those involved in the fishing industry.
On a final note-and I can see, Mr. Speaker, that my time is coming to a close-I believe the hon. member for Malpeque

October 27, 1980
Fishing Industry
(Mr. Gass) indicated that he condemns the government for dragging its heels on the east coast American-Canadian fisheries agreement. I do not know the hon. member would suggest to resolve that particular impasse. That problem lies in the hands of the Senate of the United States. At some point 1 would be interested to hear a suggestion from him in terms of encouraging the U.S. Senate to approve this particular agreement.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, 1 welcome the opportunity to participate in the debate on the motion presently before the House since I represent a constituency in Nova Scotia where more than one-third of my constituents are directly or indirectly involved in the fishing industry.
The motion moved by the hon. member for Nanaimo-Alber-ni (Mr. Miller) states, among other things:
That this House condemns the government for its failure to support the Canadian fishing industry, as demonstrated
(a) by betraying the interests in Canadian fishermen in its international
fisheries negotiations with the United States;
Later, it goes on to say:
(d) by its lack of action to enforce existing legislation protecting our fisheries.
I well remember the statement made on March 29, 1979, by the then secretary of state for external affairs, the Hon. Don Jamieson and, of course, the present Minister of Fisheries and Oceans (Mr. LeBlanc). The statement, which was released with considerable fanfare, indicated that four agreements had been signed with the United States; two relating to the Atlantic coast and two concerning the Pacific coast. The East Coast Fishery Resource Agreement established a Canada-U.S. fisheries commission and provided for co-operative management and access and entitlement to specific stocks of mutual concern.
The treaty to submit the delineation of the maritime boundary in the Gulf of Maine area to binding dispute settlement provided for the submission of a case to a five-judge chamber of the International Court of Justice for a final decision on the placement of the boundary. In the event that the International Court of Justice was unable to function under the formula mutually agreed upon by the governments of Canada and the United States, the dispute was to be automatically referred to a five-member independent international court of arbitration.
The East Coast Fishery Resource Agreement and the halibut protocol were submitted to the United States administration and to the United States Senate for its advice and consent. Although these treaties were signed by the Secretary of State Cyrus Vance and Lloyd Cutler, serving as the special representatives of the President of the United States, and by Canada's ambassador Peter M. Towe and special negotiator Marcel Cadieux, to date no action has been taken on this important matter by the United States Senate.
In my opinion this is a flagrant abuse of power by the United States Senate and today, these ineffective treaties represent the biggest single issue Canada has with any particular country. The fact that our Department of External Affairs and our Department of Fisheries and Oceans have been unable to bring any pressure to bear on the United States Senate such as would lead to ratification and approval of these treaties is a sad commentary on the relations which presently exist between our two countries.
Canada, and Canadians, stand by the agreement as signed by the United States administration. We made that fact abundantly clear to the United States senators and congressmen in Washington on Wednesday July 23, 1980. Concerned as we are over the lack of action by Washington on this important matter, the delegation under the chairmanship of Hon. Hartland Molson, assisted by Hon. Richard Donahoe and Hon. Charles Elman plus nine members of the House of Commons, representative of all parties, met with nine American senators including Senator Claiborne Pell and Senator Edward Kennedy and with 11 congressmen in order to try to clarify our position.
We pointed out that the Canadian government cannot, in effect, accept renegotiation of the agreement with the United States Senate. In our view, if amendments are proposed by the Senate these would likely upset the delicate balance achieved after a year and a half of intensive negotiations and would work to the disadvantage of Canadian fishermen since the United States terms of access would undoubtedly be increased.
We also pointed out that amendment or rejection of the agreement could have a serious effect on Canada's bilateral fisheries relations with the United States and might well raise problems which could spill over into other areas.
Moreover, since the signing of the fishery agreement an increased American effort, especially for Georges Bank scallop, has already substantially diminished the share of Canadian fishermen in that stock at a time when the stock is going through a decreasing phase of its natural cycle.
During our discussion in Washington the U.S. senators argued that the treaty should be for a limited time, rather than permanent. I pointed out to them during my remarks that it allows for renegotiating catch shares every 10 years. The Americans wanted more scallops. In fact, the amendment moved by Senator Kennedy to the East Coast Fishery Resource Agreement stated that the agreement should terminate three years from the date of its entry into force. He also proposed further restrictions on Canadian scallop draggers operating on Georges Bank. Senator Kennedy believes that the
October 27, 1980

United States should control scallop management. Unfortunately, as I speak to you tonight, the United States still has no scallop management plan for its own fishermen. They have a groundfish management plan however, and for yellow tail flounder they set a quota of 10,000 pounds to be caught between October, 1979, and October, 1980.
By July of this year, United States fishermen had caught half as much fish again, which explains why Canadian fishermen have little or no faith in any United States management plan not backed up by an international treaty.
After my visit to Washington, there are some doubts in my mind that United States representatives who are opposing the treaty understand it. Maine governor Joseph Brennan does not agree the treaty is perpetual. He says the fisheries are always changing. This viewpoint overlooks the fact that fish on Georges Bank carry no passports. They can be Canadian today and American tomorrow, or vice versa. It overlooks the fact that the two sides must reconsider quotas every ten years and that the treaty, once approved, builds in joint management and dispute settling procedures.
Today there are more and more suggestions that Canadian fishermen should start taking all the groundfish, herring and scallops they can before the Americans do. Their reasoning is that action of this type would give Canadians more fish for the time being, thus making the United States government more conscious of the need for a long-term management treaty.
I am glad to see the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. MacGuigan) in his seat tonight.-Another suggestion 1 have, if the treaties as they presently exist, are not soon ratified, would be to delink the boundary settlement from the fisheries treaty. As it is now, the boundary line treaty goes to arbitration only after the United States ratifies the fisheries treaty.
As soon as the presidential elections are over in the United States, I hope that our fisheries minister and the Secretary of State for External Affairs will go to Washington together for the purpose of recommending to the New England fishing interests, the U.S. senators and congressmen that their interests would best be served by prompt ratification of the treaties which Canada and the United States negotiators drew up with a view to protecting the stocks, as a result of which fishermen of both countries will benefit. Unless such an effort is made, Canada's fishermen will rightly share the view that this government is derelict in its duty, not only to them, but to Canadians generally.
I turn now to another contentious issue presently before the industry, namely the marketing problems faced by many large and small processors operating in Atlantic Canada. The present minister-and I regret he is not in the House this evening-has his own views concerning the industry's marketing problems. He expressed them in a rather uncomplimentary manner in some speeches this spring. These comments did not in any way help the industry in its marketing efforts, nor did they provide any solutions for improvement. To tell the indus-
Fishing Industry
try that there are possibilities outside downtown Boston, that they need to take out a wider map than the map of Massachusetts, is, if I might say so, through you, Mr. Speaker, somewhat beneath the minister's dignity. That the industry is facing some marketing problems is a known fact. What is equally true is that in some cases these problems are directly due to the actions or inactions of the present Liberal administration. When the Minister of Fisheries and Oceans refers to "solidly organized" marketing organizations which have a great deal of "clout"-and I am using his words-with which Canadians must compete, surely he is well aware that these organizations are highly subsidized by their governments.
Norway, for example, paid direct subsidies to its industry amounting to $180 million in 1979-$120 million in the first four months of 1980-and it has paid similar amounts in every year since 1974. In addition, Norway has an outstanding tariff preference in the very important European Common Market. Canadians have been selling significant quantities in Europe in spite of the tariff disadvantage we face on some major products. However, there is no doubt that the European economic community tariffs are being used in a discriminatory way against Canadian imports, and now their reference price system is also being invoked against Canada.
I would remind the minister and this government that the commercial Canadian fishing industry cannot change tariff and non-tariff barriers. Only the government has this power. It seems to me the whole weight and prestige of the Canadian government in its trade relations with the European economic community should be applied to remove these inequitable trade barriers. That is the clout needed by the Canadian fishing industry.
The minister should also strengthen the muscle of the Canadian fishing industry by using his ministerial strength against the frivolous countervail petitions aimed at Canadian exporters by American fishermens' groups. The minister should be more concerned about these matters, if not for the sake of the fishing industry, then at least for the threat that it poses for governments, shipyards and regional development policies.
Quite frankly, I deplore as loudly as possible the confrontation policies which presently appear to exist between the minister and the fishermen, between the minister and the industry and between the minister and the provincial counterparts in Atlantic Canada. In my opinion, the industry and the government, rather than confronting each other in an adversary posture, should be working together in an effort to mutually solve the problems which come under their collective powers.
One of the policies being followed by the minister of fisheries, which is seriously damaging marketing throughout the industry, is his continued policy of over-the-side sales. This spring, the ministers of our three maritime provinces expressed complete dissatisfaction with the lack of meaningful consultation by the federal government on the issue of indirect or over-the-side sales. They questioned, for example, whether the present Minister of Fisheries and Oceans has the legal author-

October 27, 1980
Fishing Industry
ity to allocate amounts of fish to foreign buyers without the approval of the provinces. They agreed there should be no direct sales involving guarantees unless there was prior consultation with the provinces, and that all conditions and guarantees offered to foreign buyers be offered to Canadian firms as well. This seems only fair, and it would place Canadian firms in the same competitive position as foreign companies getting over-the-side sale permits. The provinces also wanted any participating foreign vessel to be granted a permit from the respective provincial authority.
When endorsing these proposals for consideration by the federal government, I want no misunderstanding about my own position. I am not advocating provincial control over our fisheries. I have stated on previous occasions in this Elouse, and I repeat my stand tonight, that I firmly believe the deep sea fishery must remain under direct control of the federal government.

speechtext:
However, federal control does not prohibit provincial consultation and this is one area which can be investigated and expanded.
The present federal policy of authorizing over-the-side sales to communist countries with guarantees of extra squid, mackerel or herring to the ship, in the event its holds are not filled prior to leaving our 200-mile exclusive zone, may, on the surface, appear to be a bonanza to our fishermen. But in actual fact its over-all effect is extremely damaging to our industry. There is a growing concern today about the effect of over-the-side sales and their impact on Canadian efforts to develop markets for our fishing products, in particular, the so-called underutilized species, such as mackerel and squid. The problem seems to be that the Canadian industry keeps running into Canadian fish being sold by the Russians, or other east bloc countries, in our own markets. In fact, prospective sales have been turned down because the buyers anticipated Joint Trawlers Ltd., a Soviet company, would have an over-the-side contract in 1980 and would supply the mackerel cheaper. In fact, this has happened.
Recently I attended a Commonwealth Parliamentary Association conference in Zambia. While I was there I had an opportunity to meet with delegates from all over the Commonwealth, including some from West Africa. While speaking to a delegate from Nigeria, I learned that Nigeria used to provide a huge market for Canadian mackerel. We still sell some mackerel to that country, but we cannot develop a strong position in the market because of the competition provided by the Russians, selling Canadian mackerel which they buy through over-the-side sales in Canada. They pay more to the fishermen
than is possible by Canadian processors due to our unemployment insurance costs and high taxes. Because of their fixed overhead, they must have a certain price for their product. The Russians sell for less in order to get hard currency.
I also learned from another source that a Canadian sales team were shown Canadian mackerel in Egypt which had been bought from the Soviets. The price paid by the Egyptians was well below Canadian costs of production. Consequently, the Egyptian buyers advised that they would not buy any more mackerel from Canada unless we could meet the competition. The competition is provided by a communist country using slave labour which pays no taxes to Canada. It does not matter what prices our processors offer to the fishermen. For example, if it is ten cents a pound, the Soviets will offer 12, and if it is 12 cents a pound, they will offer 14. It is economically impossible for Canadian processors to meet that kind of competition.
The same applies to our sales of squid. Japan is the main market for this product, followed by southern Europe. Here again, Joint Trawlers Limited, a Soviet fishing company, undercuts Canadian exporters in Europe, supplying the market with Canadian squid. Japan has import quotas in place for squid, so every pound of quota supplied by the east bloc countries uses up import quotas that Canadians need for entry into the Japanese market. It is also my understanding that Canadian squid from east bloc sellers is underselling Canadian squid being offered by Canadian exporters to Japan, further damaging our position vis-a-vis the import quota.
These are only a few examples. There are many incidents like this which show that our over-the-side sales are hampering Canadian marketing and market development efforts. The effect on Canadian employment is, of course, obvious. There have been attempts to require the fishermen's groups to supply the shore plants' needs in any over-the-side arrangement, but these have not come to anything.
The Newfoundland union was permitted a foreign vessel in Black Tickle, Labrador this summer to buy cod fish-yes, cod fish-in spite of the fact there is a shore plant there owned by the province, and in spite of the fact that Fishery Products Limited, a Newfoundland company, was prepared to transfer any surplus catch to St. Anthony where the cod fish was needed. This deal was approved by the present fisheries minister on the basis that the local plant at least would be supplied, but this did not happen until the foreign vessel went aground and became a total loss.
I believe we have a responsibility to establish Canadians in a position where they can harvest, process and market the species I have mentioned without facing unfair competition from the communist bloc countries, countries that are not required to operate under the profit system but whose aim instead is to work for the overthrow of western countries and the free enterprise system. In fact, if present over-the-side sales policies continue, we must seriously ask ourselves what is the over-all aim of this government as it applies to the fisheries?
October 27, 1980

You have taken over the processing and marketing of freshwater fish in western Canada; you have taken over the processing and marketing of cod fish in Newfoundland through the Salt Fish Marketing Corporation. Are you now proposing to destroy the independent fresh fish industry in Atlantic Canada so that you will have the entire industry under your control?
If so, if this is your policy, you should come clean with the Canadian industry and the Canadian people presently involved in its development so that they can plan the best course for their own future.

speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S O. 58-ALLEGED FAILURE TO SUPPORT FISHING INDUSTRY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I welcome the opportunity to speak on this motion, if for no other reason than to bring the House up to date on the latest developments concerning the fishing industry in my province and, in particular, in my riding.
It is a sad commentary on the knowledge that many Canadians have of their country that many of my colleagues in this House, on both sides, are surprised to learn that there is even a fishing industry on the prairies. Indeed, many members of this House thought I was pulling their legs when I talked of it. Therefore, I would like to inform the House tonight that a fishing industry on the prairies really does exist. It is a multimillion dollar industry, it employs thousands of people, it is the backbone on which many prairie communities were founded and it remains so in many of them to this day.
In the year 1978-79, net sales of the Freshwater Fish Marketing Corporation, which markets all fish caught on the prairies and in the Northwest Territories, amounted to over $34 million. I realize that this figure pales beside the coastal fishing industries, but it is nevertheless significant to the areas involved. As well, one must add the sale of rough fish, private sales, sales through co-ops and so on.
For the sake of this debate, let me bring my comments closer to home. In my riding of Selkirk-Interlake, there are over 1,000 fishermen doing roughly $10 million worth of business annually. Fishing has been very important to central Manitoba since the late 1870s when the Icelanders came to settle the shores of Lake Winnipeg. The existence of a large body of water with an abundance of fish meant a continuance of a known way of life to people who had for many years fished the north Atlantic. They did encounter one unknown obstacle, ice. The north Atlantic never froze over, but Lake Winnipeg did. However, with a little instruction from the local Indians, they were able to overcome that.
In a rather ironic turn of events, three years ago a fisherman from my home town of Gimli was hired to teach Newfoundlanders how to fish through the ice. My friends from Newfoundland, I must admit, are a touch embarrassed when I tease them about having to learn how to fish from a prairie boy.
For many communities in Selkirk-Interlake, Fishing was for many years the major source of income. Gimli, Riverton, Hecla Island, Hodgson, Grand Rapids come readily to mind.
Fishing Industry
In many communities to this day, fishing is still the main business. This is particularly true in many native communities. On Indian reserves at Easterville, Grand Rapids, Little Saskatchewan, Lake St. Martin, Jackhead, Dauphin River, Fisher River and others, unemployment jumps when the fishing season ends to as high as 95 per cent. 1 think these few comments indicate just how important the inland fishing industry is. In my opening comments, 1 said that many Canadians were totally unaware of its existence. Too often it seems that the government opposite is also unaware of its existence. In his comments this afternoon, the Minister of State for Multiculturalism spoke of his government's desire to make famous world wide such Canadian fish as salmon, cod, halibut and so on. I was a bit dismayed when he left out pickerel and whitefish, or the famous Lake Winnipeg smoked goldeye. However, we in the Interlake are long used to this kind of neglect from Liberal governments.
At this point in its history, the Manitoba fishing industry is facing some very serious threats. This is not the first time it has been threatened. In the late sixties, the business was floundering badly after years of abuse at the hands of large corporations, largely American owned, which treated their fishermen employees as little better than indentured serfs. However, the establishment of the Freshwater Fish Marketing Board in 1969 brought an end to this. After a somewhat rocky start, this board brought order to the industry and a much greater degree of prosperity.
A year later, Lake Winnipeg was closed because of possible mercury pollution. However, after considerable study, this proved to be wrong and the lake was reopened. The threats to the industry today are many. As my colleague, the hon. member for Nanaimo-Alberni (Mr. Miller), mentioned in his opening comments, the Garrison diversion unit is one of them. My colleague from Skeena mentioned acid rain. This has not yet had any great effect on Lake Winnipeg, but it will inevitably take its toll.
The biggest problem has been government neglect. I would like to focus briefly on three or four areas and explain what I have in mind. One area is licensing. The system of licensing used on Manitoba lakes at the present time is very unfair to many fishermen. On some lakes there are three seasons- summer, fall and winter. Many fishermen are able to get only one licence, others two, very few fishermen have all three. It is very hard to make a living and support a family on only one licence, or two. Last winter, the Manitoba government produced a new scheme of licensing which would inevitably have meant the wiping out of many small fishermen and a return to the pre-1969 era of big interests controlling much of the lakes. During the winter months, they held meetings throughout the province to introduce or to explain this system. I suppose it is indicative of their lack of understanding that they were rather taken aback when their system met with universal opposition. They withdrew the program quickly.

October 27, 1980
Fishing Industry
I realize that licensing is administered by the provinces, but the federal government has the right to make some input into policy. However, it has not done so to date.
Another area of contention to Manitoba fishermen, and indeed to many inland fishermen, is the unemployment insurance regulations which are designed for the needs of coastal fishermen and which do not take into consideration the very different needs of inland fishermen. This is especially hard in many of the communities where there is no other employment in the off-season.
The third area is the vessel subsidy program. As many hon. members know, for many years the government provided 35 per cent of the cost of new fishing boats for fishermen. This was a very good program and it was helpful, especially to natives and to young fishermen trying to get into the business. Last summer the government of the day withdrew this program. This caused much consternation to inland fishermen and it was especially hard on natives and on those people who have only one or two licences and who really cannot afford to buy new equipment. It was also hard on the boatworks. I know of two boatworks in the town of Winnipegosis, which is in the neighbouring riding to mine, which were forced to shut down. Two boatworks in the town of Gimli have had to lay off their employees. Last fall the program was reinstated on a limited basis, but at present we do not really know whether it will continue or where it is going to go, and this is very unsettling for many fishermen in Manitoba.
The single biggest threat is one which I have already mentioned, that is, the Garrison diversion unit. Let me explain briefly what the Garrison diversion is. It is an irrigation scheme in the state of North Dakota. It is a motherhood issue, something that has been dreamed of by North Dakotans for over 100 years now. The idea is to use some of the water from the Missouri River system to irrigate the dry lands of north and central North Dakota. The benefits of this system at present are rather questionable. In order to irrigate 250,000 acres of land, 220,000 acres of land will be taken out of production. The cost benefit factor is definitely negative. However, this is not of concern to Manitobans; it is an internal North Dakotan problem. What is of concern to us is that the Garrison diversion unit as defined will link up the Missouri River water basin with the Hudson Bay water basin and as a result of this link-up through-leaching chemicals will be introduced into the Red River-Hudson Bay system, as well as parasites and strange fish.
A year ago, on the first chance I had to speak to the House, other than in the question period, I introduced to the House two of these strange fish, the rainbow smelt and the gizzard shad. Tonight I would like to add a third, the Utah chub. All three of these fish are rapid breeders, very adaptable to new environments, and would seriously threaten existing fish stocks.
Let me read from a technical report issued by the Fisheries & Marine Service in February, 1979. It is entitled "Potential Effects of Exotic Fishes on Manitoba: An Impact Assessment
of the Garrison Diversion Unit." With regard to the rainbow smelt, the report concludes:
-we believe that rainbow smelt will be successfully introduced and established in Manitoba waters . . . We believe that smelt, when introduced to Manitoba, will cause the collapse of lake herring populations in Lakes Winnipeg, Manitoba and Winnipegosis and will have a major negative impact on the lake whitefish fishery in the north basins of Lakes Winnipeg and Manitoba. Smelt will also have negative impacts on walleye fisheries in certain locales of Lakes Winnipeg, Manitoba and Winnipegosis. Declines in the abundance of higher-valued species will result in decrease in fishermen's incomes such as occurred in Lake Erie during the late 1950s.
With regard to the gizzard shad it says:
-we believe that gizzard shad will be introduced and can be established in Lakes Winnipeg, Manitoba and Winnipegosis. There are suitable environmental and habitat conditions, food supplies and spawning areas for establishment of gizzard shad populations in these waters.. . Magnitude of impact may range from minimal impact to the worst possible impact of total collapse of walleye and sauger populations in these lakes.
With regard to our new friend, the Utah chub, they say:
In summary, Utah chub have a high reproduction potential, a potential for population irruptions and likely can establish in Manitoba waters . . . Furthermore, if in Manitoba waters, Utah chub will have a negative impact on indigenous fishes and may become a nuisance to anglers and commercial fishermen (through sheer volume of catch in the nets). We expect Utah chub will compete with whitefish and walleye for food and likely displace, to a major extent, existing forage species, particularly minnows . . . Therefore, we consider this fish to represent the same potential for major impact as rainbow smelt or gizzard shad.
Now I should like to quote some figures. The report gives a table of the percentage reductions in population size. They use three figures, the lowest, the most likely, and the maximum. I will only use the most likely figures. In the Lake Winnipeg north basin, the effect on the lake whitefish will be a 50 per cent reduction; on lake herring it will be 75 per cent; and on walleye and sauger 50 per cent. In the south basin of Lake Winnipeg, the effect on the lake whitefish will be a 5 per cent reduction; on the lake herring, a 5 per cent reduction; and on walleye and sauger, a 50 per cent reduction. In Lake Manitoba, the effect on the lake whitefish will be a 30 per cent reduction; on the lake herring it will be 75 per cent; and on walleye and sauger, 75 per cent.
The end result of this potential hazard to Manitoba fisheries will be nothing short of disastrous. Let me tell you how seriously people in Manitoba are taking this. I am sure the Right Hon. Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) would not like to hear this comment, but there are people in my riding who consider the resolution of the Garrison issue to be of greater concern to this country, or at least to Manitoba, than the present constitutional issue. There can be no iFs or but's on this issue. No link-up of the Missouri River drainage basin and the Hudson Bay drainage basin can be allowed. It is as simple as that. The actions of governments in Winnipeg and Ottawa have been far less than reassuring. The Boundary Waters Treaty of 1909 is quite clear. In article 4 it says:
It is further agreed that the waters herein defined as boundary waters and waters flowing across the boundary shall not be polluted on either side to the injury of health or property on the other.
Clearly the Garrison diversion unit will break that treaty. We get statements from the state department and the executive branch that the Boundary Waters Treaty will be adhered
October 27, 1980

to, but construction crews in North Dakota continue to dig canals. Just last month a tender call was issued for the construction of the New Rockford canal which runs in the direction south of Jamestown. The New Rockford canal is completely useless unless the Lonetree reservoir is completed. If and when the Lonetree reservoir is completed, the link-up between the Missouri and the Hudson Bay systems will be in effect and the Manitoba fishing industry will go down the drain. Meanwhile, our governments rely on diplomatic niceties. The Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Mac-Guigan) knows well of my concerns on this issue. Indeed, I believe he is sympathetic and has been supportive of me and of some of the actions I have taken to oppose the Garrison project. Our ambassador in Washington and his staff have done an exceptional job within the confines of their role to express to the U.S. state department and to U.S. politicians our concerns on this matter. But, damn it, it is just not good enough. I have a premonition of the day when the first gizzard shad swims up the Red River.
On that day I see the United States state department reaffirming its position not to violate the boundary waters treaty and our government sitting there still believing the Americans. But it will be too late then.
As the motion put forward today by my hon. friend indicates, this Liberal government is indeed betraying the interests of Canadian fishermen not only on our coasts, as my colleagues earlier have said, but also on our fresh water lakes. If this betrayal does not end soon, members of this government opposite will be as welcome in Manitoba fishing communities as our friend the gizzard shad.

Mr. Speaker, I have listened carefully to the comments of my good friend, the hon. member for South Shore (Mr. Crouse). He did a good job during the few months that he was president of the Committee on Fisheries and Forestry, and I believe that we had very interesting proceedings during his term in office. 1 would like to congratulate him on the way that he managed and administered this committee during the few months of the Progressive Conservative administration.
Mr. Speaker, in reading once again the wording of the motion that we have been asked to debate today, it seems to me more and more obvious that our friends opposite have not only missed the target, but more important, that they have misdirected their shot by believing that it would be easy to show the failure of this government in the administration of fisheries and oceans, and especially oceans. If there is one area where the Government of Canada is making its presence felt, achieving remarkable results and making the rest of the world aware of the importance it places on the fishing industry, it is certainly that of ocean management. And if there is one person among us who illustrates the interest shown by the Government of Canada in this area, it is certainly the present Minister of
Fishing Industry
Fisheries and Oceans, the hon. member for Westmorland-Kent (Mr. LeBlanc).
Mr. Speaker, we must thank God that the Minister of Fisheries and Oceans of the Progressive Conservative administration between May, 1979, and February, 1980, did not keep his portfolio any longer. Everyone recalls what happened when the large trawlers entered the Gulf of St. Lawrence. Ail the in-shore fishermen associations of Quebec, New Brunswick, Prince Edward Island, and even Nova Scotia appeared before the Committee on Fisheries and Forestry to express their dissatisfaction with this policy of the then minister.
Mr. Speaker, it is not a secret that our country is bordered by three oceans. We have the longest shoreline in the world. The sea which surrounds us and over which we extended our country's jurisdiction for fisheries to 200 nautical miles from our shores in January, 1977, for most people-and also, no doubt, for our friends on the other side-has resources, secrets and mysteries still unknown to us. To quote the words of another great parliamentarian, Sir Winston Churchill, when he was describing the Soviet Union: The sea, a great unknown, a mystery within an enigma-
Mr. Speaker, when it created the Department of Fisheries and Oceans in 1977, the government took on an ambitious task. Not only did it take over the responsibility for managing fisheries, it also took on the responsibility for managing the oceans over which it had already affirmed its jurisdiction. Of course there were relationships between ocean sciences and fisheries, but there was much more than that. There was also the challenge of the eighties, a challenge which extends to the responsibilities of the coastal states for the development of off-shore resources as well as the systematic and responsible development of renewable resources. It was, as it can be easily seen, a considerable task and an exceptional challenge.
As we say, the absent are always in the wrong. And I know today that the Minister of Fisheries and Oceans is not among us. He had some other commitments. Today he is on the Pacific coast, the bearer of good news to those who are in charge of fisheries in British Columbia. For once, we will prove the proverb wrong. It is not by chance that the minister was entrusted with the portfolio of the Fisheries and Oceans after our return to power in February last.
Let us recall a few facts which are all to his credit. The minister who comes from the maritimes had assumed the responsibility of Fisheries and Oceans when he was minister of the environment. It was not long, however, before he was concerned exclusively with fisheries and oceans. The fisheries file at the time was faced with enormous difficulties. My hon. friends opposite will doubtless remember how we dealt with this painful situation in 1974. The industry was coming out of a period of plenty which had lasted several years. Suddenly, it realized that the halieutic resources were not inexhaustible, that the natural environment was in the grip of serious pollution problems, that the fishing areas could be the object of

October 27, 1980
Fishing Industry
stubborn dealings between the users, in short, that all was not well in the best of all possible worlds, and that it had better get hold of the situation, impose regulations, and especially obtain from all interested parties the assurance to carry out their activities in a responsible manner, in anticipation of the future.
This is the assignment which the minister took on with determination and success. Our hon. friends cannot say anything to the contrary. The hon. member for Westmorland-Kent got back his portfolio after a short break. There are many people from the industry and the users who have expressed their satisfaction. Finally, Mr. Speaker, the captain was taking back the helm of the ship he himself had built and that he knew well how to sail through the tormented seas he knew so well. Thanks to the work of his officials, the administrators and the scientists of his department, the minister has been able to demonstrate with conviction that this industry that some considered of little importance had its place in our country. Through reasonable management practices and through responsible development and expansion programs based on precise data, he proved that this industry was capable of becoming prosperous.
The first to acknowledge this fact are the fishermen themselves, Mr. Speaker, coming from nowhere or just about, they again found themselves lords and masters of the seas and the oceans. Furthermore it is with a renewed pride that they say that they are fishermen and that they have undertaken without cease to roam a vast expense they had been given the keys, namely the oceans and the new economic zone of 200 nautical miles.
Now, what are the challenges ahead in the eighties? In fact, Mr. Speaker, the fishing industry had to undergo a change not only to maintain its present position but also to develop at the same rate as its competitors to be able to respond to new needs.
Fishing has evolved from a simple family business to a sophisticated industry requiring up-to-date equipment and efficient processing methods. It has recently been able to meet new market demands for non-traditional species of fish, which meant the acquisition of new production techniques.
What is the responsibility of the present Canadian administration? When dealing with ocean management, it is addressing a threefold task:
(a)	First, under present conditions, dealing with the management of underwater oil operations.
(b)	Second: Preserving a very precarious balance by waging a fight against sea pollution.
(c)	Last but not least, managing Canadian fisheries within the 200-mile limit.
To make matters clear, I will recall the criteria by which management performance is rated. Mr. Speaker, I was very pleased, a moment ago, on hearing my good friend, the hon.
member for South Shore, state that the administration of fisheries in the Atlantic ocean, within a 200-mile zone, must be the exclusive jurisdiction of the Canadian government and 1 told the hon. member to go and see his good Progressive Conservative friends in Newfoundland and impress upon them, as well as on the hon. Premier Peckford, that the management of Atlantic fisheries must remain under the exclusive jurisdiction of the Canadian government. I laud my good friend, the hon. member for South Shore, for his statement. For once, I am in agreement with him and perhaps with you also, my good friend, the hon. member for British Columbia; and we see here the hon. member for Malpeque (Mr. Gass) who supported this motion admit that he agrees with this policy of the Canadian government and especially with that of the hon. Minister of Fisheries and Oceans. In the field of jurisdiction of the Canadian government, the responsibility-and I am not saying that it should be shared but at least the main responsibility- for the management of the fisheries in the Atlantic area should be maintained.
There will be the cumulative amount of statistics compiled in another area. Furthermore, there will be all the effort of co-ordination of an efficient management system; this combined effort with regard to research in every discipline is directed to the integration of all those efforts to the benefit of the people who are expecting results, the individuals themselves.
That we should be faced with problems of production is easy to conceive; however, there is more. There are problems of transportation, equipment, training of manpower and also this nuisance of our time, problems of pollution. These problems can come up in many ways: a breakage somewhere and we are faced with raw materials being spread in the natural environment. When we reach the stage of processing, or usage we are faced with masses of deleterious gases released in the air. I am thinking of acid rain. I am just giving you an outline, of course, but I want to call your attention to that aspect of the problem which did not escape the Canadian government and which is a source of concern especially for the Minister of Fisheries and Oceans, the monitoring of the environment. This has been translated into a series of programs and specialized activities following the adoption by the Canadian Parliament of legislation concerning the protection of the environment which for the time being meet the needs which have been recognized.
In November, 1978, Canada and the United States signed an agreement on water quality in the Great Lakes. This agreement is aimed at eliminating almost totally all dumpings of toxic substances into the Great Lakes and setting a new limit on the permissible quantity of phosphorus for each lake; joint municipal and industrial programs on dumping of polluting products into the lakes are to become operational according to a very tight schedule. During 1979-80 the federal atmospheric environment service completed a study on sulphur contents in the air over a three million square kilometres area
October 27, 1980

in eastern Canada, including the maritime provinces and a major portion of Quebec and Ontario. The Department of Fisheries and Oceans was actively involved in programs whose findings have revealed a high frequency of acid rains over all that wide territory.
Mr. Speaker, I must say that I am proud to be a member of the subcommittee on fisheries and forestry which is now studying the effects of acid rains in Canada. I will now comment briefly on fisheries management in Canada's 200-mile zone. We often hear critics of the Canadian government and especially of the Department of Fisheries and Oceans declare without any misgivings that the government has done nothing for the management of fisheries and oceans in the 200-mile zone.
In fact, Mr. Speaker, the staff has increased considerably at the Department of Fisheries and Oceans since 1976 and national outlays earmarked for scientific research on fisheries totalled some $112 million annually. In conclusion I should say that the Canadian government has done a lot for oceans and for the administration of fisheries in Canada. It is certainly not a failure as the opposition claims, but indeed this political party, this government has done its best for the management of fisheries and oceans and the minister and member for Westmorland-Kent deserves full marks for that.

Mr. Speaker, I should like to thank the hon. member for Nanaimo-Alberni (Mr. Miller) for placing this motion on the order paper for debate today, because it gives us an opportunity which is all too seldom afforded to bring to the fore some of the problems in the east and west coast fisheries.
In thanking him I would not say I agree entirely with every single word he has put into his motion. In fact, I take exception to the word "betraying" which appears in the first paragraph because I think it is a very strong word. The negotiators I know in the international field, particularly those negotiating with the United States, are not the kind who betray. They may not properly take certain things into account; perhaps that is a better way of putting it. I would say the motion should read as follows:
That this House condemns the government for its failure to support the Canadian fishing industry, as demonstrated (a) by its failure to take into account all the interests of Canadian fishermen in its international fisheries negotiations with the United States-
Now the very first one of these I would tie in with section (d) of this motion because the government has demonstrated all too obviously a lack of action to enforce existing legislation and its claim to the 200-mile limit. There has been altogether too little effort made by this government to live up to and enforce the extra maritime territory which was acquired by the decision to extend the fisheries zone out to the 200-mile limit. Therefore I think we do have a way of uniting sections (a) and
Fishing Industry
(d)	of this particular resolution, and if possible I may be able to get at one of the others.
One of the things I do wish to speak about this evening is the manner in which international agreements between Canada and the United States are concluded and what happens to them once they are concluded. We have heard from the hon. member for South Shore (Mr. Crouse) the problems related to the fishing agreement on the east coast. I was not at that special meeting in Washington when a group of members from both sides of the House, and from both Houses, went to Washington to explain to the United States Congress the Canadian position on the ratification procedure related to that particular agreement. However, I was present when the matter was first initiated in San Diego during the visit of the Canada-U.S. parliamentary group. At that meeting the member for St. John's East (Mr. McGrath) suggested that rather than take up all the time of the meetings in San Diego-there were other topics we were discussing at that time-it might be desirable for a special group to go to Washington. It did that in July.
We read this morning in a press release of recommendations made to the two governments by negotiators on the west coast which it is expected will be adopted as a treaty in due course. There are four, five or six elements in this agreement which I think are worth recording here. One is the recommendation which deals with the problem of interception, that is, which country may catch which fish. Conservation of all five species of Pacific salmon was taken into account during negotiations and recommendations were agreed upon as to who should be able to catch whose fish. Catches of salmon spawned in one country but caught in another should be limited. According to this press release it is generally agreed-as it has been agreed for years-that the division should be equal, although at the present time Canadians take about two million U.S. salmon each year while Americans take five million Canadian-bred salmon. That inequity is one of the problems which the negotiators have been attempting to deal with, and it is one worth noting.
Another matter which was included in the recommendations dealt with the situation which arises when one country wants to allow more salmon to return upstream so as to encourage a greater stock production. In that case there would be a proportionate decrease in the take on the American side resulting in the Americans proportionately reducing their take. Accordingly, there would be a smaller catch of American-bred salmon. Then there is the question of control over the Fraser River, and, finally, the recommendation that Canada should receive credit for fish spawned in northern British Columbia and Yukon rivers but caught in U.S. nets. That is a very special problem because of the panhandle and because of the flow of the rivers. The salmon enter the Yukon River, in American estuaries, swim up the Yukon and eventually breed in Canadian territory. At another Canada-U.S. interparliamentary group meeting we did see some of the escapement going through the fish ladders up in Whitehorse.

October 27, 1980

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S O. 58-ALLEGED FAILURE TO SUPPORT FISHING INDUSTRY
speechtext:
We on the west coast face a real crisis and it is important that we take the time to discuss the matter. My colleague from Nanaimo-Alberni has put forward a comprehensive criticism of the government's failure to support Canada's fishing industry. Among other things, he mentioned its failure to stand up to the United States in negotiating our fishing treaty and its failure to refuse to allow them to push us on the boundary issue.
The hon. member pointed out that the continuing high interest rate policy of this government is an added burden on fishermen who are already facing serious problems of high payments on their boats. He pointed out the government's failure to limit the amount of gear that is going into the water, with the result we continue to have more and more gear chasing fewer fish. The hon. member for Nanaimo-Alberni pointed out the government's failure to develop our research capability at the very time we face growing management difficulties with the fishing industry. Finally, he pointed to the serious neglect of fish habitat.
It is interesting to hear what the Minister of Fisheries and Oceans (Mr. LeBlanc) had to say in an interview while in British Columbia last spring. The newspaper report I have here quotes him as saying:
There are some problems on the west coast but in the past it has shown it can take the knocks.
The fishing industry on the west coast is taking very serious knocks and unless the minister and the department get to work it will receive a knock-out blow from which it will never recover. Along with other members of my party who are vitally concerned about the future of this resource and the industry in British Columbia, I plead with the minister and his department to take some positive action that will alleviate the situation.
Within the broad outlines of the criticism established by my colleague from Nanaimo-Alberni, I would, first of all, like to make some remarks of particular interest to my constituency, Cowichan-Malahat-The Islands. Second, I would like to point to some of the problems which the native Indian people of British Columbia face with regard to fishing. Like fishermen from all along the British Columbia coast, many of those in Cowichan-Malahat-The Islands have experienced a disastrous year. Depleted stocks, low catch prices, rising costs and high interest rates have all worked together to keep fishermen from breaking even, let alone making a profit or even making their wages.
Ten years ago the salmon catch in British Columbia was 280 million pounds. Last year it was half that at 140 million pounds. This year I understand we will be very lucky if we break 100 million pounds. Obviously, something very serious is wrong with the way in which the department has managed the resource. The people who are paying for this mismanagement are the people who have been led to invest money in boats and in gear with the hope of making their livelihood from fishing. They are caught in a vicious cycle of boom and bust.
I submit that the Department of Fisheries and Oceans must manage the resource much better and that we should not be
Fishing Industry
subject at the mercy of periodic slumps. There is need at the present time for immediate help so that fishermen do not lose everything for which they have worked over the past few years. Right now their livelihoods are in jeopardy as they try to make the high interest payments on their investments in boats and gear. Unless action is taken to protect these fishermen, this industry will become controlled more than ever by large corporations, and as anyone who has looked at the industry knows, this has been continuing trend over the last 50 years, more and more power being gathered into the hands of fewer and fewer corporations.
Along with my concern for fishermen who are making high payments on their boats, I would like to make a plea for the shore workers. I would request that the government consider bringing in some kind of special legislation to lower to eight the number of weeks that shore workers must work in order to qualify for unemployment insurance benefits. It is important that these people, on whom the industry depends, on whom our economy depends, should not have to bear the entire brunt of the boom and bust cycle which is a result of the government's failure to act. They should not have to assume the entire burden. I think it would be right and fitting if the government shared that burden.
When I look around my constituency, Mr. Speaker, I become greatly concerned at the government's failure to protect the fish habitat. I welcomed the assurance given the other night by officials of the department that it would continue to protect the fish habitat in the Cowichan estuary regardless of what the provincial task force on the Cowichan estuary will say when it finally reports. We have been waiting for that report for more than two years.
There seems to be a determination on the part of some forces in British Columbia to further industrialize the estuaries. Of course, these are easy places in which to put industry but industry in such sensitive areas would destroy the very basis of our fishing industry and the basis of our present and future prosperity. The federal department should have the gumption to oppose this kind of industrialization which can only lead to the degradation and destruction of the fish habitat. There was federal representation on the task force. We are waiting for the results of its investigation to see whether the department is willing to protect the fish habitat or whether it is going to bow before the demands of those who want to industrialize the estuaries and who have no concern for the habitat of fish. People come to me to talk about the Fraser River and how important it is to the economy of British Columbia-indeed, to the economy of Canada. We regret the failure of this government to protect the Fraser River and keep it from turning into the world's largest sewer.
While the Fraser River is important-and I do not want to underestimate its importance-I want to emphasize that there are numerous smaller rivers and streams which, combined, have a very great fish producing capacity. In my constituency the government has been just as neglectful of these small areas

October 27, 1980
Fishing Industry
as it has been of the Fraser River. For example, the Cowichan River is in serious trouble at the present time and this is a river that has a fairly major impact on our fisheries. The study done for the Cowichan estuary task force two years ago pointed out that this river is important to Indian food fishing, to commercial fishing and also to sports fishing. I walked the banks of that river with an old-time fisherman last spring and saw how some of the side channels have been allowed to silt over and how the debris has accumulated. These side channels need to be cleared so that the fish can spawn there again. I was shown some of the log jams and the destruction they cause. As the water comes down river, it hits the log jams, and forces its way into other channels and develops swift currents that eat away more and more of the bank. As a result there is less space in which the salmon can spawn. What used to be one of the best salmon rivers in British Columbia is being destroyed by neglect. What we need is some kind of joint federal-provincial arrangement to take care of this river and others like it.
I was disappointed to learn that of the $28.5 million budgeted for the salmonid enhancement program in 1980, only $1 million was put aside for natural enhancement. Too much of the emphasis in the salmonid enhancement program is laid on big engineering projects. When the program was introduced three or four years ago, departmental officials held hearings in small and large communities throughout British Columbia to find out what the people thought was the most necessary aspect of it. The message in one community after another, was that emphasis should be placed on natural methods of enhancement and on stream clearing. Instead, the department has chosen to establish the big engineering projects. Of that $28.5 million allocated to the salmonid enhancement program, only $125,000 is available for public participation projects and small stream work.
In my constituency, the Cowichan Indian band has a salmonid enhancement projet but it is hard pressed to find the funds to carry out the work. In this House we have spoken about the problem of Indian unemployment. This is a program which could help the salmon industry and put people to work at the same time but the funds do not seem to be available. The government has suggested that the band could apply to the Canadian Community Development Project for funds.
Of course, the government knows full well that the money allocated for these projects in all of western Canada, is but a drop in the bucket and does not begin to meet any of the real needs-either of stream clearance, the hatchery project, nor to speak of the need for employment. It is just a cynical public relations move.
1 am concerned about the government's failure to protect the fish habitat from spraying by chemicals about which we do not have sufficient evidence, such as the krenite spraying that took place in British Columbia during last summer.
My next area of concern relates to Indian fisheries, Mr. Speaker. I welcomed the announcement made a week ago that $4.2 million would be made available to Indian fishermen in special aid. I think this recognizes an important crisis. Unless help is given now, even more Indian fishermen will be squeezed
out of business. Since 1969 when the Davis Licence Limitation Plan was introduced, the Indian people have been squeezed out of the industry. For example, one group of Indian people on the west coast of Vancouver Island found that between 1973 and 1976, the number of Indian-operated trollers declined by 54 per cent. These figures indicate very dramatically how the Indian people are being squeezed out.
We should recognize that a crisis exists at the present time and, we should also recognize that the Indian people face a continuing crisis. We know that 59 per cent of the Indian population is under age 25 yet there is no program to provide jobs for these people, and they are not able to enter the fishing industry. Traditionally, the Indian people on the west coast have been referred to as the salmon people-people who depended on the ocean and on the annual runs of salmon even before there was a commercial industry there.
This has been their culture and life. They are being squeezed out of it. It is important we recognize the significance of this crisis and make money available to help them. We need money for the economic development of the fishing industry on the coast. I thought the Indian fishermen's assistance program was helpful, but there have been severe criticisms of it. Some of the Indian people have asked whether it was right that one small group of people should be allowed to develop themselves while others were being squeezed out of the program. More of the Indian organizations are asking for programs to help the whole Indian community to develop Indian community wellbeing rather than simply to develop individual well-being. We need training programs for our Indian people, so they can become involved in more of the complex areas of the fishing industry.
Perhaps we should also be looking at a very old method of catching fish by the use of fish traps which the Indian people used. I realize it is heresy to talk about this in our time because we are so committed to the idea of free enterprise in the fishing industry, to the idea of using more and more gear and burning up more and more oil chasing after fish. However, maybe there is a possibility that the old method of establishing fish traps at the mouth of a river, through which mature fish come would eliminate the trouble of catching all the small fish which must be thrown away. Then we would be able to manage individual streams and develop the resource for the entire community. We would be able to take some kind of rational approach to the fishing industry. Perhaps in five or ten years more people might realize that fish traps are a more sensible approach than the present gear-intensified craziness which is presently destroying our resource and making it more difficult for people to make a living from it.

speakeroldname: Mr. Brian Tobin (Humber-Port au Port-St. Barbe):
subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S O. 58-ALLEGED FAILURE TO SUPPORT FISHING INDUSTRY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am particularly pleased to speak to this motion because the fishery is the lifeblood of my province and it is vital to many of my constituents in Humber-Port au Port-St. Barbe.
October 27, 1980

What we have before us is a motion which condemns the Government of Canada for its failure to support Canada's fishery-condemns us to where, I do not know; nevertheless it condemns the Government of Canada. The motion goes on to accuse the Government of Canada of betrayal, or of following a course of anarchy in its fisheries policy; also it complains of a lack of change in policy and finally it accuses the government of failure to enforce those policies already described as a betrayal to fishermen in the first place. I would suggest the motion in itself is a contradiction in its terms.
Let me suggest to the hon. member in the New Democratic Party who put forward this motion that I respect his right to present it. 1 respect his right to raise his concerns about Canada's fishery. In fact, I agree, with many of his concerns and I am sure the Minister of Fisheries and Oceans (Mr. LeBlanc) would agree also. I am concerned about large corporations getting control of a bigger chunk of the fishery. I am concerned about companies that would like to monopolize the fishery at the expense of our fishermen. I am concerned too about the threat which industry is posing to Canada's fishery every day.
In my own province, the most stringent environmental guidelines will have to be applied to protect our fishery from offshore oil and gas development. However, I would respectfully submit to my colleague opposite that to offer constructive advice, in other words, to move a motion for the consideration of this House which might bring about important change, would be more productive and positive than any negative motion.
It is my intention to clarify some of the matters raised in this House today by opposition members as they relate to the fishing industry on the west coast of Canada and in my own area on the east coast.
First, dealing with the west coast of Canada, I shall start with a few statistics. Traditionally, the west coast fishing industry represents approximately 35 per cent of the total revenue generated by the fishing industry right across Canada. It is responsible for the direct employment of roughly 22,000 people. The five main species of Pacific salmon are sockeye, chum, pink, chinook and cohoe and they are, of course, the backbone of the fishing industry off the coast of British Columbia. As such they represent a bountiful renewable resource.
Over the years, salmon have provided a good living for many west coast fishermen. Annual income of $50,000 to $70,000 have not been uncommon in recent seasons. If honourable members have any doubts about the state of prosperity of the west coast fishing industry, they have only to cast their eyes over fishing fleets in such places as Steveston or Prince Rupert and contemplate the investment of tens of millions of dollars tied up in boats and gear, much of it the latest and most advanced technology on the market.
Unfortunately, and it is unfortunate, the situation in 1980 is not as buoyant as it has been in previous years. My information is that despite some unexpectedly high chum catches in recent weeks, salmon landings generally in B.C., up to the end
Fishing Industry
of September, were running 22 per cent below those for the corresponding period in 1979. Extrapolating that trend to the year end indicates that 1980 salmon landings will range between 52 per cent and 91 per cent of the ten-year average, depending on the species, with the over-all total at about 77 per cent of the ten-year average. That is not good news. Predictions are that the total landed value of this year's salmon catch will amount to approximately $103 million. This is a 36 per cent drop from the 1979 value of $160.5 million and it is much below the four-year average of $140 million in the period 1976 through 1979. The fact that salmon prices are from 10 per cent to 20 per cent lower than last year is a contributing factor to the over-all decrease in landed value. I might point out that catches of salmon fishermen in the northern part of the province were actually higher than in 1979, both in the troll and the net fisheries. The fishermen who are doing poorly this year are mainly those fishing off the southern part of British Columbia, particularly the trollers.
Making this a worse-than-usual year for the industry in B.C. was a strike earlier this year. Indeed, there was a strike in my province, which will no doubt reflect itself in the figures at the end of the year. Because of the strike by the herring fishermen in British Columbia, most of them did not participate in the previously lucrative roe herring fishery this year.
What will the impact of this downturn be on the average west coast fisherman? Certainly there will be a decrease in the net incomes of many fishermen in 1980. In some cases, this could lead to repossession of vessels-God forbid-where the owners are caught in a credit squeeze. However, because of the healthy earnings of past seasons, there is every expectation that most west coast fishermen will be able to cope with the situation and get through until next season with a little belt tightening.
I have been assured that officials of the department are continuing to closely monitor the impacts of current economic conditions on Pacific fisheries in order to assess whether special assistance may be necessary.
