speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I rise on a point of order. Could the hon. member who is speaking answer a short question at this time?

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S O. 58-ALLEGED FAILURE TO SUPPORT FISHING INDUSTRY
speechtext:
I will accept the hon. member's question when I am finished.
Although the fisheries economic picture on the west coast this year is not as bright as one might have wished, it does forcefully point up the unpredictability which characterizes the fisheries harvest and the extreme complexity of managing the fisheries resource. And nowhere is this task more complex than in the salmon fishery on the west coast.
As an example of this complexity, one might take the Fraser River system which has more than 40 different stocks of chinook salmon, whose movements once they leave the river are still not fully understood. Each stock is unique with its own set of characteristics which allow it to migrate the required

October 27, 1980
Fishing Industry
distances, to develop in temperatures indigenous to its spawning area and generally to survive in the environment of its home river. For example, McGregor River chinook travel nearly 500 miles to their spawning grounds, compared with Capilano stocks which only swim about four miles upriver. Egg incubation periods differ from stock to stock and so do the rearing times of young fish.
The Fraser is probably one of the most complicated systems that fisheries management personnel must cope with. This is due to the fact that the commercial fleet is concentrated in the areas through which the Fraser stocks must pass, coupled with the long and perilous journey up the main stem of the river which the fish must make to reach their spawning grounds. The intense fishing pressure, the natural hazards facing the salmon's survival and encroachment on the habitat of the salmon as a result of various industrial activities and competing resource uses, all add to the problems of fisheries management. Not only are a few stocks declining in the face of this onslaught, but some are in danger of extinction.
Flowever, our fisheries managers are not ready or willing to throw in the towel in their fight to save and hopefully, enhance, the Fraser chinook stocks. For them and for the Minister of Fisheries and Oceans, the struggle to save the salmon takes on aspects of a religious crusade. They know what they are trying to do is worth while and that the results of their labours will benefit not only the present generation, but generations yet unborn.
A key element in this fight is a massive tagging program which over the next few years is hoped will generate the information that fisheries biologists need to effectively manage the commercial, sport and native food fisheries, and to plan future enhancement programs.
Fast year nearly 600,000 three-month-old chinook fry from British Columbia rivers and hatcheries, had a fin clipped off and a coded wire identification tag inserted in the nose cartilage. When sport fishermen catch one of these fin clipped fish, they are asked to turn the heads into depots across the province. The commercial catch is sampled for marks in the processing plants. The nose tags are removed and the number codes read and recorded. In this way it is possible to identify the date and origin of the fish and gain information on where, when and how the fish was caught, thereby assisting biologists in charting the migration patterns of the different stocks of salmon of British Columbia.
The statistics from tagging will also allow fishery managers to pinpoint more accurately the times and places when a Fishery should be closed down in order to allow stocks to escape the fishermen's nets or hooks and return to the river to produce the next generation.
However, establishing a fishing plan which will ensure adequate escapements to each river is made even more difficult when stocks from a variety of rivers are mixed together in the same fishery. For example, if a stock from a highly productive river and stock from a river that is not as productive are fished together, too large a percentage of the less productive stock may be caught, thereby furthering the decline of that stock.
A similar problem arises when stocks from an artificial enhancement facility and "wild" or natural, stocks are fished together. This is because enhancement facilities obtain much higher survival rates than occur in the wild. With cohoe salmon stocks, for example, survival rates of 80 per cent from the egg to smolt stage-that is when they first venture into the ocean-are common in hatcheries. By contrast only about 11 per cent or 12 per cent of the cohoe which incubate and rear in the stream in totally natural conditions will survive to the smolt stage. Thus if natural and enhanced stocks are fished together, the fishery manager must choose between the harvesting of fewer fish from the enhancement facility than necessary, or the harvesting of too many wild fish.
I must apologize to hon. members if I have become too technical in attempting to explain what the fishery manager is up against when involved with the west coast salmon fishery. My sole intention is to provide a better insight into the complexities of the matter. And at that, 1 must admit that I have only just scratched the surface.
The opposition motion seeks to condemn the government for alleged lack of action to devise and implement revised policies to regulate the industry or to enforce existing legislation protecting the fisheries. Certainly as far as the west coast of Canada is concerned, there is little to substantiate such allegations.
Earlier I made brief mention of the problems of safeguarding the habitats where salmon breed and grow from degradation or complete destruction as a result of various industrial activities such as logging, construction of hydroelectric dams, dredging, dumping of wastes, mining operations and so on.
Obviously it makes little sense for the federal government to invest millions of dollars in salmon enchancement schemes to increase the supply of salmon if there is no control over assaults on the basic habitats of the stocks-the cradle of the runs, as it were. For this reason the Department of Fisheries and Oceans has placed a high priority on its habitat management activities, and nowhere more so than on the west coast.

The federal government investment in the initial seven-year phase has been set at approximately $150 million. It is the government's intention to continue this funding, based on the success of the initial phase, to bring about the required objectives.

In economic terms, the objective of the salmonid enchancement program is to increase the landed value of the salmon harvest from the current yearly average of $160 million to $400 million, in 1980 dollars, by the year 2000. This will be achieved by allocating the increased production to its best use and by undertaking cost-effective programs to increase the quality of fish products.

I repeat, however, that a motion which merely condemns but offers no positive and constructive advice is not good enough. I would suggest that my colleague in the New Democratic Party come back with another motion which makes some concrete suggestions. I would then support his motion.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, thank you for this opportunity to make some remarks in connection with the motion condemning the government for its neglect of the fishing industry. It provides me with an opportunity to make some general remarks about the great importance of the east coast fishery to Nova Scotia and the Atlantic provinces.
First, I should make it clear that in my constituency of Halifax West, less than 5 per cent of our work force is employed in the fisheries industry. Nonetheless, it is a matter of great importance to all of us because in the fishing industry in Nova Scotia we see part of our hope for the future. That industry, along with developments in the field of energy and
Fishing Industry
marine transportation, will bring us, we hope, to a new era in the 1980s.
Let me begin a discussion of the fishing industry in Nova Scotia by listing some facts which underline the magnitude as well as the importance of our industry to the whole of Canada. We rank fifteenth worldwide but first in export sales of fish. There are over 100,000 people directly employed in fishing, and this accounts for $1.3 billion in export sales. That compares favourably with export wheat sales which amount to approximately $2.2 billion. Canadian fish production has an estimated worth of $1.6 billion, and at least $1 billion of this is earned on the east coast where most of the production is centred in Nova Scotia and Newfoundland to the extent of about 80 per cent of the total. There are 600 fish plants along the east coast and they have an effect on over 200 communities.
In the short time remaining to me, Mr. Speaker, let me speak more generally about the fishing industry. First of all, we must note that it is a world-wide industry and that Canada is only a part of it. For that reason, we must deal with other nations and other jurisdictions in order to achieve our great potential in the fishing industry. When I mention the worldwide involvement of the fishing industry, I am mindful of the fact that no treaty affecting the scallop fishery and the fishery on Georges Bank has been signed between the United States and Canada. We along the east coast of Nova Scotia urge the Department of Fisheries and Oceans to take action in this respect. Any delay will cause the disruption of the industry and potential irreparable damage. We deal with other foreign states. Recently one of the assistant deputy ministers in the department brought public attention to the fact that a new treaty must be negotiated with France which will affect the cod allocations in the Gulf of St. Lawrence to prevent the fishing industry operating in the Gulf of St. Lawrence from being jeopardized. We are very conscious of the world-wide connections of the industry and we urge the Minister of Fisheries and Oceans (Mr. LeBlanc) to be conscious of it as well.
As well as dealing with other nations, the Minister of Fisheries and Oceans, in his role as supervisor of the fishing industry in Canada, must deal with the provinces, and, as we all know, that has caused a great deal of grief and concern. We in Nova Scotia support the position that the federal authority must take total responsibility for the fishing industry. That is not to say that the provinces should not be consulted in matters of vital interest to them, particularly, as I have mentioned, in the matter of the allocation of the Gulf of St. Lawrence fish stocks.
In 1976, by action of the federal government, Nova Scotia-based fishermen were precluded from entering into the Gulf of St. Lawrence for the purpose of utilizing northern cod stocks. That situation was remedied in 1979 and an allocation was made in the Sydney-Bight area just outside the traditional Gulf of St. Lawrence area. This is a very important segment of the Nova Scotia fishing industry where 1,000 metric tons of cod are caught, producing 35 jobs and around $750,000 in revenue. It has been said that the Nova Scotia fishing fleet

October 27, 1980
Fishing Industry
could easily take 23,000 metric tons of cod fish without affecting the over-all industry, fish which, instead, are taken by France and other foreign nations.
1 do not need to remind the House what a tremendous economic liability we suffer in Nova Scotia from not having access to the Gulf of St. Lawrence stocks. It is up to the minister to resolve these federal-provincial problems. He can only resolve them by conducting negotiations with those concerned, not by confrontation or by putting down those who are legitimately in the fishing industry, whether it be inshore of offshore. But that, I am afraid, is not the course which the minister has pursued in the past. He has said, and I have the quotation here, that he is not running a winter works program, that he cannot react to the needs of the fish plant workers and the employment problems in areas which are dependent on the fishing industry. That is the kind of remark which causes difficulty and destroys understanding, and for which the minister must take responsibility.
Last Sunday I was watching the proceedings in the House as re-telecast on the CBC and I saw the hon. member for Essex-Windsor (Mr. Whelan) making a particularly earthy speech, typical of a person using earthy language. My son, who is only 11 years old, was there listening with me and he asked me, "Who is that?" I said, "That is the Minister of Agriculture", to which my son said, "Thank God he is not the minister of fisheries". But I had to say to him that I am not at all certain that the Minister of Fisheries and Oceans possesses a greater understanding of his portfolio than does the Minister of Agriculture, and certainly he lacks the knowledge which it is imperative for him to have if he is properly to supervise the fishing industry in Canada.
I should like to take this opportunity, Mr. Speaker, to draw attention to some of the problems of the fishermen in Nova Scotia and elsewhere on the east coast. They are the victims of the lack of a clear licensing policy on the part of the federal government. There are part-time fishermen who have licences and do not fish, but there are also full-time fishermen who cannot get licences and who cannot upgrade their equipment and their vessels because of confusion over licensing. This must be remedied immediately. The Minister of Fisheries and Oceans has told us that in 1981 he will introduce a new fisheries licence policy, but we have no guarantee that it will be any better than the last.
Another concern of the fishermen in my area is that the government should clarify its policy on loans for vessel construction. Anyone who has delved into this matter knows about the confusion caused by the size of boats and the great number of years before which they qualify for replacement. Action has to be taken in this respect.
With regard to small-craft harbours, the government and the department has a budget of $15 million for this item. But do you know, Mr. Speaker, that they cannot even put a light on a wharf in a small-craft harbour so that the fishermen can utilize the wharf at night, in the early morning and when the sun goes down at six o'clock? A wharf costing thousands of dollars is not much use if it remains unlighted in order to save
the federal treasury $100 or $200. This must be changed and we must start paying attention to our small-craft harbours.
There are many other matters which need mentioning- some of them were covered by the hon. member for South Shore (Mr. Crouse). There is the matter of direct sales which has destroyed the squid industry. We must find other ways to get a fair price for our fishermen. There is the matter of aquaculture, in which Norway is way ahead of us. They are already producing tons of valuable fish species through an aquaculture process. With regard to research, we welcome the fact that notwithstanding the closure by the Minister of Fisheries and Oceans of the fisheries lab, National Sea Products and H.P. Nickerson have formed a company to develop fisheries research. The name of the company is Fishes Resource Development Limited. I hope the minister will give the company some assistance because research is such an important segment of the fishing industry.
In manufacturing, we are spending $130 million on purchasing fish equipment outside Canada. This, too, must be changed. We have to develop an equipment manufacturing sector.
I see that the clock has reached ten. I will terminate my speech by warning the minister that if he does not take action, the motion against him will indeed be supported on all sides of the House.

subtopic: STATUTE LAW (MILITARY AND CIVILIAN WAR PENSIONS, COMPENSATION AND ALLOWANCES) AMENDMENT ACT, 1980- INQUIRY RESPECTING REDUCTION OF PHASING-IN PERIOD FOR VETERANS' WIDOWS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on Monday, October 20, as recorded in Hansard at pages 3822 and 3823 I put a couple of questions to the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Lamontagne) in his capacity as the Acting Minister of Veterans Affairs. I am grateful to the minister for being here tonight so that we can
October 27, 1980

discuss again for a few minutes the important issue involved in the question 1 put to him.
I always hope that in one of these late shows one might get a favourable answer which tells us we are winning in an important cause. If the minister is not able to do that tonight, at least I hope he will leave the door open so that it will not be long before we do win what I regard as a very important issue.
As hon. members are aware, for about 50 years we had a provision in the Pension Act which denied a pension as of right to a widow of a disabled veteran if that disabled veteran's disability pension was below 48 per cent. Some of us feel that that provision was wrong through all of those 50 years; we finally got rid of it earlier in this session. Indeed, it was the last activity on the part of the former minister, the Hon. Daniel MacDonald, on July 9, when what was then Bill C-40 was put to the House. It has since become chapter 19 of the statutes of 1980.
That bill did some other things as well, but the main thing it did was to bring to an end that 48 per cent rule and to establish a regime under which pensions can be paid to widows in cases where the veterans' disability rate was below 48 per cent.
That was good. That was an important, red letter day. It was a landmark decision on the part of the Parliament of Canada. However, there was in it a provision which for many widows will spoil it because many of the widows I have in mind will not live to draw the pension to which they are entitled under that piece of legislation.
The reason is that there was included in the bill a phasing-in period which means it will take six and a half years before all the widows given entitlement under that legislation draw their pensions. The phasing-in works on the basis of what the rate of pension was. This month, October, pensions are payable if the disability rate was 38 per cent or more. In April it will come down five more points, and then each year after that it will come down five points until finally, in 1986, the piece of legislation will be fully in effect.
1 think this was most unfair. I think it was thoughtless and that this House should not have been asked to include that phasing-in provision in this piece of legislation. I am sure-I know-that the former minister did not like it. In fact, before the House met on April 14 he indicated that he hoped to bring back the bill regarding widows' pensions which had been introduced in the previous session by the hon. member for Victoria (Mr. McKinnon) when he was minister of veterans affairs but that he hoped to improve it, particularly with respect to the phasing-in period. However, when he brought down the bill, it was the same bill we had had from the hon. member for Victoria. The result is that in this month of October about 1,500 widows will qualify for the pension we passed in July. But that leaves 24,500 widows who have to wait six months, a year and a half or up to six and a half years. Surely that can be corrected.
Adjournment Debate
I know the argument put forward is that we must consider the costs. The statistics we have been provided show that in the first full year of operation this plan will cost about $6 million and that in the final year when all the widows are covered it will cost about $42 million a year. That is a difference of $36 million a year. To any of us as individuals that is a lot of money, but around here it is not very much. As for the envelope system they have over there, there is nothing sacrosanct about it, that each department gets only so much money. The Acting Minister of Veterans Affairs who is also the Minister of National Defence could recommend to the government a transfer of $36 million a year from the budget of the Department of National Defence to the Department of Veterans Affairs and the people in national defence would not know he had done it. They would have to leave the wing off one airplane or something like that.
There is no logical argument for this. Surely there is a place for compassion and understanding. These women are older women, and I hope we will find a way either to shorten that phasing-in period or to get rid of it altogether. I have had a lot of experience around here writing letters to constituents and to persons all over Canada. 1 have never had more difficulty that I have in writing to widows who are 75, 77 or 78 years of age who tell me they have written in about their pensions and they have had a letter back from the appropriate official in which he says, "Yes, your entitlement has been established, but please write us again in 1985 and we will see that you get the pension in 1986." How does one say that to a woman who is 77 or 78 years of age and who thought that Parliament had given here entitlement to a pension as a widow of a disabled veteran?
The minister said the other day that the department would take care of urgent cases. The government always puts it that way. We are not asking for charity or welfare. We are asking for what is their right. As I say, I hope the minister will say yes tonight. I know it is in his heart to do so. If somebody is keeping him from doing that, at least I hope he will leave the door open for making this needed change to this session's Bill C-40.

PENITENTIARIES-HOSTAGE-TAKING INCIDENTS-DANGER POSED TO GUARDS-INQUIRY AS TO GOVERNMENT ACTION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on October 14, 1980, I asked the Solicitor General what he proposed to do about the situation at Dorchester Penitentiary in the province of New Brunswick. My question followed an incident which had occurred the weekend before which resulted in the death of William Morrison. Mr. Morrison, as you may know, was taken along with another guard as a hostage and in an attempt to rescue both Mr. Morrison and the other guard, Mr. Morrison met his death. This was a most serious and tragic event and one which concerned not only the members of this House but all those involved in the corrections system. However, the incident and the resulting death were not without warning as far as the Solicitor General (Mr. Kaplan) is concerned. Just a few days before, on October 9, acting under Standing Order 43, I asked the House to instruct the minister to conduct an investigation of the activities that were taking place at Dorchester Penitentiary. This was not the first time I had addressed questions to the minister on the subject. In June and July of 1980 there were rumours that there were difficulties in Dorchester Penitentiary which resulted from the transfer to that institution of dangerous persons who had been incarcerated in the British Columbia Penitentiary and other federal institutions. The Solicitor General, in response to this complaint, indicated that such was not the case. But I, nonetheless, gave to the minister my concerns about dangerous offenders who were incarcerated in Dorchester Penitentiary, and in other federal institutions. I asked the minister whether he did not think that all the hard core inmates across the prison system who had demonstrated that they were violent and dangerous should not be gathered into one group and sent to one institution for incarceration. The minister, in reply to my question during the proceedings of the justice committee, said he could not dismiss the hope in connection with any human being that he would not change his attitude and decide that he would like to go straight. The minister went on to suggest to me and to the members of the committee that it was right and proper to keep hard-core, dangerous offenders in institutions where they were in contact with other prisoners, notwithstanding that most people would have given up any hope of reform on their part. He said that one of the objectives of the prison system was to keep inmates, however dangerous, as close as possible to ties they had with the street so that rehabilitation could be reinforced if the inmate did choose to go straight.
The three inmates who caused the incident at Dorchester which resulted in the death of William Morrison can hardly be taken to have made such a decision. All three had been previously charged and convicted of murder and had been denied parole except after the minimum period of 25 years. Yet they were abroad in that institution.
My purpose in speaking again on the matter tonight is to implore the Solicitor General to take some action that will protect prison guards and other employees of our federal
October 27, 1980

national security institutions from dangerous and violent prisoners. The minister said in response to my question that he had now begun to prepare a list of names of those offenders across the system who are the most violent and dangerous and who represent the greatest threat to order in those institutions.
This action comes too late for William Morrison and his family, as well as for other guards who have had such difficulties with other prisoners in the past. Surely, some action must be taken now. It has been said to me by persons who work in the prisons that since the abolition of the death penalty and the imposition of long periods in which a prisoner is not eligible for parole the situation is quite different in maximum security institutions from what it was. Prisoners have no hope of release within a reasonable period of time. They are under no constraint whatever and can suffer no greater punishment than has already been inflicted upon them.
The minister must change his policy, gather up the violent and dangerous prisoners in our institutions and take some action. Perhaps the best action would be to open the doors of the prisons to public scrutiny so that we might know what is going on in those federal institutions. We have asked for an inquiry, and 1 would repeat our request that the Solicitor General allow a public, independent body to examine our prison system to suggest what I regard as necessary reforms.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada; Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of State for Social Development
subtopic: PENITENTIARIES-HOSTAGE-TAKING INCIDENTS-DANGER POSED TO GUARDS-INQUIRY AS TO GOVERNMENT ACTION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I think members on both sides of the House will agree with the hon. member for Halifax West (Mr. Crosby), that it was a most serious, tragic event that happened at Dorchester. On Tuesday, October 14, 1980, the hon. member raised this issue requesting information with regard to the number of incidents which have occurred in federal institutions and asking what action the Solicitor General (Mr. Kaplan) intends to undertake to respond to these warnings.
The hon. member further asked why the Solicitor General had rendered the correctional officers and staff helpless in the face of obvious danger. I respectfully submit that that is an overstatement, albeit in the form of a question. The Solicitor General rejects the allegation that he has rendered the correctional officers and staff helpless. As he stated to the House on Tuesday, October 14, the correctional service is at present preparing a list of the names of those offenders across the system who are the most violent and dangerous and who represent the greatest threat to order in the institutions.
We are not dealing with a tea-party. Everybody in a correctional institution is there because he has committed a crime, probably several crimes. It is individuals of this type we must sort out. It is a very difficult job. Once the list has been completed, consideration will be given to additional programs within the institution to further protect the correctional officers. We all agree that they have a very difficult job to perform, one that most people do not want to undertake.
Adjournment Debate
All incidents are reported direct to the Solicitor General and a security inquiry is conducted on each serious incident. The service attempts to learn from these incidents by analysing the circumstances and applying solutions, when possible, on a national basis in order to prevent further occurrences.
More specifically, definite action has been taken in terms of the difficult problems which have plagued Dorchester Penitentiary in recent months. The Inspector General, at the request of the Solicitor General, conducted inquiries into every major incident at Dorchester. In that vein, the Solicitor General should have in his hands very soon, the latest report on the tragic hostage-taking incident which resulted in the death of correctional officer William Morrison. These inquiries will no doubt recommend certain actions to be followed. The management team at the institution did develop a plan of action to review and reinforce security measures throughout the institution. In late August, the institution was locked up in order to facilitate cell by cell searches as well as several surprise searches of cells. New security fences were installed inside Dorchester's walls; posts and post duties were also reviewed. Unfortunately, however, the latest tragic incident took place.
The experience acquired as a result of the designing and implementation of this plan will be of benefit to the service on a national basis. Nevertheless, we are not dealing with an exact science; we are dealing with an art. Unless we take every offender out and shoot him, these problems will continue. That is the only way you will not have any repeaters-when they create the offence, just shoot them. That is the guarantee of not having a repeater.

Mr. Speaker, on May 12 I put a question to the Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development about the subsidy housing program for Indian bands. I wanted to know when the amount of $12,000 per unit would be increased. This question resulted from a number of representations I had received from Indian bands across the Algoma-Manitoulin area.
As everyone knows, the whole Indian housing program has been a top priority in terms of need. A recent survey indicated that 26 per cent of Indian families are doubling or tripling up in order to find accommodation, and 25 per cent of the homes

October 27, 1980
Adjournment Debate
on Indian lands require urgent repairs. A number of other problems of health and safety have been implicated in the lack of adequate housing for Indian bands and that is the reason for the number of representations I have received from the bands in my constituency.
On July 31, the minister announced an increase in the allocation of financial assistance for Indian housing projects from $12,000 per unit to around $20,000 or $22,000 per unit, as well as a certain amount of increased assistance from Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation.
The statement by the minister on that date indicated that this increase in subsidy from $12,000 to approximately $22,000 would be supplemented by job-creation programs. That is really where the problem starts, because although the minister indicated the increase in his press release, the amount of assistance available through the Department of Employment and Immigration has dropped drastically. Although additional funding is available through the Department of Indian Affairs and Northern Development, the kind of financial assistance available for the labour and construction of band housing has dropped drastically. For instance, in the Algoma constituency our allocation this year for native projects under the Community Development Program was only $115,000 for some 12 Indian bands and some 4,000 to 5,000 status Indians. In past years, for instance, in 1979-1980 under the transitional LEAP program, of the $923,242 we received, much of it went to housing. In 1978-1979 under the Canada Works program, of the $721,386 we received, much of it went to housing and in 1977-1978, we received $743,902. It is very apparent from the kinds of representations I am receiving from bands throughout my constituency that there is inadequate funding for the labour portion in the construction of homes.
It is important for the Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development (Mr. Munro) who, after all, has the final responsibility for Indian housing and for direct employment programs throughout the winter to thoroughly review the matter and see that additional funding is provided, otherwise the serious housing problem which now exists will not be corrected and a lot of people will be unemployed who should be employed under the direct employment programs over the winter months.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on July 31, 1980, the Minister of Indian Affairs and
Northern Development (Mr. Munro) announced that an additional $20 million would be allocated this fiscal year to improve Indian housing on reserves. At that time the housing subsidy was increased from a maximum of $12,000 per unit to a maximum of $22,125. This amount is supplemented by a transportation allowance of up to $7,000 for construction of housing units in very remote areas of Canada.
My hon. friend from Algoma has, I believe, 17 or 18 reserves in his riding and I know he is always concerned about the plight of the Indian. As far as job-creation opportunities are concerned, my friend should also realize that right now it is not just the Indian who is suffering, but also the white man with closures such as those at Chrysler and Massey-Ferguson. Notwithstanding this subsidy, the Indian still does not have enough to build proper housing. I am familiar with the housing that is being built. Therefore, CMHC has made available loans over and above the subsidy. The construction that is being done in my friend's riding is being done quite well, according to CMHC and national housing standards.
There is a thrust toward community-based planning and development of Indian self-government which I am sure, Mr. Speaker, you are well aware presents quite a problem. How far does the government go into telling the Indian what to do? How far does the Indian go in as governing his own affairs? There has been a compromise of sorts following this concept. For example, when a band obtains approval for the construction of ten houses, capital subsidies for ten units will be forwarded to the band. The band will then allocate the subsidy dollars to band members or to band-owned housing projects, or a mixture of both. This will be done in accordance with the chief and council's perceptions of who needs housing units the most. The band's only commitment is to see that at least ten housing units are built for an input of ten units of housing subsidy.
In 1980, after consultation between the Department of Indian Affairs, Indian associations, Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation and other departments and agencies of the government, a comprehensive set of recommendations concerning this subject was developed. The government is continuing to review means to revise an on-reserve housing policy and program to seek the most effective means to overcome the present backlog of new housing units required and the larger number of existing units in need of repairs.
